items.title: The Funeral of Ratko Mladić: Between Political Rally and Opportunistic Grotesque Commentary Serbia formally bid farewell to Ratko Mladić without a state funeral. Yet the state arranged the transport of his body, the military took part in the ceremony, the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church officiated the service, and ruling-party structures organized “spontaneous” gatherings along the route. The funeral thus became a political event and an opportunity for the authorities to instrumentalize a dead body to send messages to both domestic and international audiences. Srđan Milošević
items.summary:
The state-organized funeral of Ratko Mladić, commander-in-chief of the Serb forces during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has rightly drawn public attention in Serbia and internationally. Mladić was a military commander who, at the time of his death, was serving a life sentence imposed on him in 2017 by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia for war crimes and crimes against humanity, as well as for genocide in Srebrenica. The funeral drew attention because of its sheer scale and its de facto state character, which fell short of a fully official form in only a few details. The direct involvement of the Serbian state was most visible in the army's active participation in the memorial events and the burial. A barely concealed state tribute to the deceased was evident in the presence of a number of government ministers, attending "as private individuals." In the spirit of the "symphonia" between altar and state leadership, the funeral service was conducted personally by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church. The ruling party, which long ago usurped the state and its mechanisms, organized its phalanxes to "spontaneously" greet, from overpasses and along the road, the vehicle carrying Ratko Mladić's body from Belgrade airport. The body had been flown there from the Netherlands on a Government of Serbia aircraft, accompanied by the Minister of Justice.

In this commentary, I will first point to several precedents showing that such conduct by the Serbian government and part of the Serbian public is not unique in Europe, although it does display certain unsettling specificities. I will then consider the broader circumstances that made such an event possible without stronger public resistance. Finally, I will turn to the specifics of the current political context that served as a catalyst for the inappropriate spectacle we have witnessed.

Precedents

Several elements together constitute an event with no substantively comparable precedent in recent history. These are the extent of the participation of the Serbian state and its institutions in the funeral of a person convicted of crimes under international criminal and humanitarian law, the officiating of the highest church leader, and the presence of several thousand citizens. The Archive of Public Gatherings (Arhiv javnih skupova), an organization that monitors public assemblies, estimated attendance at around 16,000. Admittedly, there have been comparable situations, but their "controversiality" falls short of the event discussed here. I do not intend to suggest any equivalence in terms of ideological profiles, the scale of crimes, or any other parallels, since such comparisons always carry a risk of anachronism or relativization in historical accounts. Even so, one dimension is clearly comparable across different contexts: the attitude of the state and the public toward persons convicted of crimes at the moment of their death.

As is well known, the senior Nazi military and civilian officials sentenced to death at Nuremberg were for the most part left without a known grave. By contrast, individuals who served fixed prison terms and completed them were, after their deaths, usually buried within the family circle, with modest funeral rites. One exception, which comes somewhat closer to the funeral of Ratko Mladić, is the funeral of Admiral Karl Dönitz, Hitler's successor at the head of the Third Reich. However, the parallel lies primarily in the event as a public (not state) manifestation and in the presence of several thousand citizens and Dönitz's comrades-in-arms, Wehrmacht veterans. Any involvement of the German state was entirely absent in this case. Moreover, the German authorities of the time explicitly ordered that Dönitz be denied all the military honors that an officer of his rank would otherwise have been entitled to. No active-duty service member was permitted to appear at the funeral in uniform, an order some officers ignored. In short, the funeral of Karl Dönitz, who was convicted after the end of the war, was a relatively large event. It included the appropriate church ritual and an honor guard of veterans holding high military decorations, and it took place under the sign of informally expressed high esteem for the deceased top Nazi official. Yet somewhat earlier, in 1973, one of the field marshals of the Third Reich, Erich von Manstein, had been buried in Germany with military honors; he had been sentenced to a multi-year prison term in 1949. There was a clear difference in the treatment of these two convicted Wehrmacht officers. Although both held high rank, Dönitz's membership in Hitler's innermost circle and in the leadership of the Third Reich was an insurmountable obstacle to granting him official posthumous honors.

A more recent example is the funeral of Croatian general Slobodan Praljak, who was convicted in The Hague. General Praljak's body was transported to Zagreb under special measures and with the utmost discretion. A private farewell at Mirogoj cemetery was held among family and closest friends, in accordance with Praljak's own wishes. However, the main public act of tribute was organized by the Croatian Generals' Assembly (Hrvatski generalski zbor), an association of retired generals, at the Vatroslav Lisinski concert hall in Zagreb. The commemoration was attended by around 2,000 people. Among them, though not in the capacity of official state representatives, were the then Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, the Minister of Croatian Veterans, and the Deputy Speaker of the Croatian Parliament. Numerous other members of parliament, former senior political officials, and generals also attended, including several prominent figures from Croatia's military and veterans-political establishment. On the same day, a senior church dignitary (a bishop) celebrated a requiem mass, attended by numerous generals, war veterans, and other public figures from Croatian politics. The active military was not involved in the event. Even the participation of a choir made up of active service members was not approved, precisely so that the active military would not be associated with the convicted man.

There have been other comparable examples in the past, especially if one includes figures who remained unconvicted for crimes that can clearly be attributed to them. The circumstances were generally similar: over time, the retributive character of the attitude toward such a figure weakened, and conviction and punishment usually did not extend post mortem, in the form of a secret burial or the scattering of ashes at an unknown location. The exception in this respect is Rudolf Hess, whose remains were first buried at a known location and later relocated so that the burial site would not become a gathering place for neo-Nazis.

As far as Serbia is concerned, a precedent had already been set with the burial of General Nebojša Pavković in the Alley of Distinguished Citizens. That funeral had a somewhat more official character than Mladić's, with the highest military honors and the official presence of state officials, including an envoy of the President of the Republic. With the funerals of Nebojša Pavković and Ratko Mladić, given the way these events were organized, the Serbian authorities and the part of the Serbian public that took part in them have gone further than in any previous comparable case. They did so in terms of state involvement, scale, and above all the publicity given to these events.

The Broader Context

The main political and social precondition for the state's deep involvement in organizing the funerals of convicted military commanders from the 1990s wars in the former Yugoslavia is a persistently encouraged and widespread belief in Serbia. According to this belief, Serbs were the greatest victims of those wars, and all convictions of members of the Serb side are anti-Serb fabrications or tendentious exaggerations. This is the message continuously communicated by every source of public authority: state officials, most of the intellectual public, and the Serbian Orthodox Church. Dissenting voices are not merely drowned out. Everyone who dares to speak on these issues contrary to the privileged view is publicly discredited, accused of anti-Serb activity, and subjected to aggressive propaganda and verbal violence, which occasionally escalates into physical violence. One journalist has even received a death threat.

In such an environment, any meaningful debate that might call into question the "sacred truths" is not only futile but impossible. These truths concern the alleged lack of objectivity, political bias, anti-Serb orientation, and instrumentalization of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Court of Justice in The Hague. Both judicial institutions established that the crime in Srebrenica constituted genocide, a finding firmly rejected in Serbia by most of the public that holds any view on the matter. Moreover, even the criminal offence of genocide denial has been drafted in Serbian criminal legislation very carefully and deliberately, so as to exclude the possibility of punishing denial of the Srebrenica genocide. The concept of "dealing with the past" has been promoted almost exclusively through the activities of civil society organizations. In Serbia it has produced very limited results, reduced to individual insights and an almost privatized sense of reverence for the victims, without any public articulation.

The attitude toward the Srebrenica genocide is a particularly telling illustration of this atmosphere. Even when it is "acknowledged" that a crime took place, incomparably more condemnation is directed at those who characterize that crime as genocide than at those who committed it or who deny it, even while glorifying those responsible. Individuals and organizations that consistently advocate respect for the judgments of the Hague tribunal are disqualified far more harshly and far more often than the perpetrators of the crime are criticized, whatever the specific legal qualification may be. And one question in particular arises: why is the qualification "crime against humanity," the alternative qualification of the Srebrenica crime, so much more "appealing" to genocide deniers? What would change in their attitude toward the crime if its qualification were different? These questions are, unfortunately, rhetorical.

For decades, the main "argument" in Serbia that the Srebrenica crime was not genocidal in character has been that Bosniak women and children were not killed, or that the ethnic group of Srebrenica Bosniaks was not destroyed as a whole. The argument is meaningless if only because the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide provides that genocide can be committed against part of a protected group, a point on which the courts have given very detailed reasoning. It is sometimes claimed that the Srebrenica crime was an act of retaliation for the killing of the Serb population. This, again, is an argument without any legal relevance: genocide can be committed even as an act of defence, and retaliation hardly merits discussion. In general, the legal reasoning is very little known to the public, while historical and national-emotional content is widely manipulated. This approach presupposes, of course, the complete public discrediting of the relevant international courts. Under such circumstances, legal argumentation is simply irrelevant.

Under such circumstances, and with the exception of Srebrenica, the attitude toward crimes for which Serb forces and their commanders are responsible is characterized primarily by near-total public silence in Serbia. Domestic court verdicts for war crimes are probably the least communicated output of any state body. Cooperation with the Hague tribunal is implicitly understood as an imposed obligation, a kind of international blackmail that Serbia accepted because it had no other choice. This has produced an atmosphere in which every member of the opposing side's armed forces is implicitly a criminal, while every member of the Serb forces is either innocent or all but forced into committing a crime by various turns of circumstance. The usual mantra involves an "objective" confesion that "there were crimes on our side too." However, knowledge of those crimes, or any unequivocal ethical distancing from them, is almost entirely absent, apart from the trite and unconvincing "condemnation of all crimes." How exactly does Serbian society confront these "crimes of ours"? What exactly is the ethical distance being established from, when both the crimes and their perpetrators are at best unknown to the public, while the known ones are excused in every possible way? What real effect does an abstract condemnation of "all crimes" have, without any concreteness that would give the position meaning, awaken empathy with the victims, and take a clear stance on the act itself and its perpetrators?

At the root of this attitude toward the wars and the crimes which were committed lies a perspective whose deep entrenchment is inversely proportional to its ethical and intellectual shallowness. This is the unconditional privileging of national-identity commitments, which are placed above every universal ethical principle. In terms of values and ethics, the national not only precedes every other consideration but becomes the only recognized value, even more so the greater its divergence from other considerations. Few, of course, will openly admit this, but the vast majority live out this lamentable proportion, blissfully convinced of the moral and ethical superiority of their own group. This unquestioned belief  is not relativised in the slightest. On the contrary, it is reinforced by the abstract phrase "there were crimes on our side too." This "generous" phrase serves only one purpose. It strips the prior belief in one's own moral superiority of the implausibility, the absurd unconvincingness, and the almost psychopathic detachment from reality that its absolutization inevitably entails, even from the perspective of the most impartial individual. In reality, however, the cognitive mechanism of this construct functions precisely without any concrete content behind that admission.

None of the above necessarily applies to the majority of society. It is in fact unlikely that most people sincerely participate in such a construction of reality. A model of conformism, combined with consciously chosen or unconsciously adopted indifference, is a far more convincing explanation. The problem for society, however, lies in those moments when circumstances force people to take a position. At such moments, there is no one to effectively oppose the privileged paradigm.

The Specific Context

Serbia's current ruling structures are not merely beneficiaries of the situation described above; they are among its active creators. The ruling clique's media machinery continuously, persistently, daily, and around the clock reproduces content that reinforces ethnocentric and moralizing nationalist attitudes on every socially relevant issue. In this way the ruling structure achieves two goals: the complete marginalization of opposing views, and the sidelining of those actors who claim to represent the same principles more authentically. In this respect, the government and its nationalist alternative are structurally engaged in the same task and share the same views. The specific current context in which Ratko Mladić's funeral should be viewed is largely shaped by their concrete relationship.

Ratko Mladić's funeral should therefore be viewed in light of the context outlined above, with current political circumstances in Serbia acting as a catalyst that further accentuated clearly recognizable tendencies. The ruling political organization is facing its strongest challenge ever from a political grouping built on a catch-all principle, which has managed to win over a large number of right-leaning voters. Until now, the current regime had managed to distribute this segment of the electorate among several obviously "satellite" political groupings that posed as the opposition. In the new balance of power, the regime lost this "ace up its sleeve," so an important aspect of its campaign has been to strengthen its own position as radically right-wing. In this respect, Ratko Mladić's death was a more than welcome opportunity for the regime to gain a political advantage among a large part of the right-leaning electorate. The regime quite literally exploited Mladić's death in The Hague and staged a morbid political rally. Regime media broadcast it, with the fitting tears of on-call analysts and salvos of praise for the president and his party for consistently standing by the "Serbian hero." Not a single word was said in the media about the absence of Serbia's president from this political funeral. This was evidently a line that, out of international considerations, the president did not dare to cross, despite his chest-thumping claims that he fears no one and nothing in these relations. Vučić himself offered the official explanation that he would not attend the funeral because of a meeting with the President of Uzbekistan.

The welcoming crowds for the vehicle carrying Mladić's dead body, organized on overpasses and along the route from Belgrade airport to its destination, point to coordination between state bodies and party phalanxes. How else could these groups have known the time, manner, and route of the transport? They were made up of familiar faces, the kind seen at every rally of the ruling party or in the squads of provocateurs who attack anti-government protesters. By lighting flares, displaying banners, and through their overall iconography, these groups sent society a clear message that they were acting in concert with the regime, which was giving the "hero" such a magnificent welcome. The same images dominated the funeral itself, multiplied by the participation of an almost exclusively male crowd, which also points to a kind of orchestration. However much the funeral of a military commander may be a "male event," such a minimal presence of women who might feel the need to pay their respects to the deceased also seems "unnatural." Can women not be admirers of such a "national figure"? Somewhat unusual on the front line, women are hardly as unexpected when it comes to paying last respects to a person they revere, even a general.

Finally, the current regime also found Mladić's funeral useful as an opportunity to send a message to external actors. The regime made it clear that it can easily play the card of nationalist frustration alone. Aware that this choice poses a challenge for Europe, regardless of the balance of power, the regime deliberately put Western balancing to the test. The West must weigh the unacceptability of an event such as Mladić's funeral against its interest in integrating Serbia into the Western political, economic, and security framework. Correctly judging that this interest exists, the regime keeps pushing the boundaries of its own conduct within Serbia, testing what Western actors are prepared to accept or tolerate.

In short, Mladić's funeral has so far been the furthest extent of the regime's divergence from Western actors, a divergence whose purpose is primarily domestic, but which is at the same time part of the tradition of boundary-pushing in relations with the West. On Sunday 4 October, around 156 million Brazilians will elect a new head of state. Citizens will not only be deciding on the offices of president and vice-president: they will also be electing 27 governors and their deputies, the entire Chamber of Deputies, two-thirds of the Senate, and the members of the state legislatures. The presidential run-off will take place on 25 October. 

A total of twelve candidates are standing for the presidency. However, the decision will be made in the second round between the incumbent President Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. These two politicians epitomise the deep divides that not only split Brazil but also characterise the whole of Latin America: the far-right and pro-American camp versus the social-democratic camp with its focus on the Global South. Although polls show that the majority of the Brazilian population wants an end to polarisation, it has not been possible to put forward a moderate conservative alternative.

Which Issues Are Dominating the Election Campaign?

Internal security and the fight against crime are at the heart of the debates. Voters are also concerned about future relations with the US and differing interpretations of patriotism.  Furthermore, a complex corruption crisis at the Supreme Federal Court (STF) is casting a shadow over the election campaign. The allegations also target Alexandre de Moraes – the very judge who is regarded as a symbol of democratic resilience and who put the masterminds behind the attempted coup of 8 January 2023 behind bars. This could also cost Lula crucial percentage points. 

Economic issues, by contrast, are playing hardly any role. Whilst the Brazilian economy is producing solid figures, the current government has failed to capitalise politically on these successes.

What Might Potentially Change in the Coming Parliamentary Term?

Lula da Silva’s advanced age (80) highlights how urgently the Brazilian left needs to modernise and usher in a generational change. The country therefore faces a truly pivotal election in 2030. Until then, the current crisis of confidence in the Supreme Federal Court (STF) threatens a key pillar of democracy, whilst the countless contradictions and the lack of fundamental debates are weakening the Workers’ Party (PT) from within.

Within federal politics, policy shifts are likely to be less significant than hoped for. The composition of Congress is unlikely to change much. The divisions run along familiar lines of conflict: unchecked versus controlled exploitation of natural resources; radical versus gradual disenfranchisement of Indigenous peoples and Quilombolas (descendants of escaped enslaved people), particularly in relation to mining projects with global implications; intensified versus reduced discrimination against minorities and poorer sections of the population; and the dismantling of social policy versus attempts to further strengthen the rule of law.

Significantly more noticeable changes are to be expected in foreign policy. Here, different approaches clash: a self-assured foreign policy versus a more submissive one. On the one hand, the aim is to play an active role in shaping the policies of the Global South in forums such as the G20, BRICS and UN Climate Conferences (COPs). On the other hand, there is a risk of subordination to US claims of hegemony in Latin America – for example, within the framework of the US security initiative ‘Shields of the Americas’. As a result, Brazil might fall silent on the regional and global stage.

The victory of a far-right federal government threatens to put civil society and progressive forces under immense pressure. An existing ‘agents’ law’ – similar to legislation in other countries in the region – could be implemented swiftly. This would cut off foreign funding and restrict the scope for action of progressive actors. Only time will tell to what extent global networks of democratic actors can mitigate this development.

What Does This Mean for Brazil, the Region and Europe?

In Brazil, entrenched power structures continue to shape developments. Interest-driven networks block genuine change. To illustrate: around 20 per cent of the national budget flows directly through MPs and senators to their constituencies, serving clientelist interests. This mechanism is controlled by the so-called Centrão – a conservative coalition of around eight parties with shifting alliances, in which agribusiness is strongly represented. The crucial question is: how much longer will this Centrão coalition be able to withstand the pressure from the far right and the encroaching organised crime? 

There is a great deal at stake, both regionally and globally. Brazil is one of the last countries in the region not to be governed by a right-wing government. A victory for Flávio Bolsonaro would completely shift the balance of power: the region would come under US influence almost in its entirety. This would see the Monroe Doctrine implemented in a new form (Donroe) and the ‘Shield of the Americas’ security alliance activated. In terms of foreign policy, Latin America would lose its voice in global forums such as BRICS or the G20. Instead, authoritarian governments would dominate the scene. For the European Union, a change in power would have serious consequences: it would lose an important partner on key issues such as trade and climate policy, as well as on initiatives to reshape the global order.

This Election Is Also About Addressing the Inequality Gap

Much of the debate is also reminiscent of Germany – above all the call for a strong, stable centre. To counter the Lula-Bolsonaro polarisation in the near future, democratic political forces must reposition themselves, together with civil society. Members of both houses of Congress also have a role to play. They wield enormous power and must fulfil their legislative responsibilities in order to safeguard the balance of power within the state. Why is this so difficult?

At its core, this election is also about addressing the inequality gap: the top one per cent of the population earns ten times as much as the average; estates of over 1,000 hectares continue to account for 45 per cent of the total agricultural land – and it is precisely these large landowners who make up over 80 per cent of the members of Congress (449 out of 513). 

These figures illustrate how far we still have to go to achieve genuine representation of the ‘political centre’, if by that we mean the centre and the majority of society. Lula da Silva stands for the fight against poverty and hunger and thus aims to pursue policies for broad sections of the population who, however, have hardly any voice in Congress. This closes the vicious circle of Brazilian democracy: a parliamentary majority that governs without regard for the interests of a large part of the population.
items.title: Brazil Votes: Where Is the Divided Country Heading? Analysis On 4 October, Brazil will elect a new head of state. Our office director Regine Schönenberg analyses what is at stake globally and why neither Lula da Silva nor Flávio Bolsonaro would change the country’s entrenched power dynamics. Regine Schönenberg

At the heart of Tirana, 38 remarkable and threatened species have taken monumental form. Presented on Skanderbeg Square, the new glass mosaic of the Albania Is Biodiversity campaign makes visible something Europe has yet to fully recognise: Albania is one of the continent’s great ecological treasures.

Biodiversity sustains the natural systems on which all life depends. Plants, animals and microorganisms keep ecosystems functioning, secure our food supply and provide clean air and water. Biodiversity is not a luxury. It is the foundation of our existence.

Yet European nature is in deep crisis. According to the European Environment Agency, 81 per cent of habitats assessed under EU nature legislation are in poor or bad conservation status. Wetlands, dunes and coastal ecosystems are under particular pressure. Intensive land use, urbanisation, infrastructure development, pollution and climate change are fragmenting ecosystems and accelerating the loss of species and habitats.

Across much of Europe, this damage has accumulated over generations, leaving natural habitats smaller, more isolated and less resilient. However, this is not the whole European story. The Balkans still contain landscapes of a scale, continuity and diversity that have become rare elsewhere. We therefore need a new narrative for this region. The Balkans are not merely Europe’s periphery. They preserve something that Europe increasingly lacks and needs for its future.

This is precisely why Albania matters

Albania covers only 28,748 square kilometres, less than 0.3 per cent of Europe’s surface area. Yet it contains an extraordinary concentration of plant and animal life. More than 350 bird species have been recorded here. The country provides habitats for emblematic and endangered species ranging from the Balkan lynx and Egyptian vulture to the Dalmatian pelican and Mediterranean monk seal. Albania is an ecological powerhouse for Europe.

The country owes this richness to the remarkable variety of its landscapes and climate zones. Mediterranean and Central European influences overlap. Mountains rise steeply from the Adriatic and Ionian coasts. Free-flowing rivers, ancient forests, alpine meadows, lakes, wetlands and lagoons form a connected mosaic of life.

Albania also lies on the Adriatic Flyway, a key migration route between northern Europe and Africa. Migratory birds depend on its wetlands and lagoons to rest and feed during their long journeys. These places form part of an ecological network that extends far beyond national borders.

Yet Albania’s natural wealth is by no means secure in the long term. Speculative real estate investment, tourism development insufficiently guided by environmental considerations, the increasingly intensive use of natural areas and climate change are placing its coasts, rivers, wetlands and mountain landscapes under growing pressure. Albania still has the opportunity to preserve what, across much of Europe, can now be recovered only through complex and costly ecological restoration.

Together with PPNEA, Albania’s oldest nature conservation organisation and BirdLife International’s Partner in the country, we launched Albania Is Biodiversity in 2023. The campaign stands for a new way of understanding Albania and the Balkans.

For the campaign, artist Kleidi Eski brought Albania’s remarkable and threatened species together in a reinterpretation of the iconic mosaic on the façade of Tirana’s National Historical Museum. The image first appeared in 2023 as a temporary intervention on Skanderbeg Square. It has now been transformed into a monumental glass mosaic.


Hundreds of thousands of individual pieces come together to create a single image of interdependence. Like an ecosystem, the work draws its strength from the interplay of different elements. It invites us to see Albania and the Balkans with new eyes.

European integration cannot simply mean that candidate countries adapt to Europe. Europe must also recognise what these countries contribute to our shared future. Albania brings free-flowing rivers, ancient forests, coastal wetlands, local knowledge and extraordinary biodiversity. These values belong at the heart of European integration. Europe will prove the credibility of its green and democratic promises not only in its current member states, but in how it recognises and protects the natural commons of future members.

The accession process offers practical means to translate this principle into policy. European environmental standards should apply throughout that process. The cumulative effects of infrastructure and tourism investments on ecosystems must be carefully assessed. Independent local conservation organisations need reliable support, and intact habitats should be protected before their loss makes costly restoration necessary.

Implementing this agenda requires lasting partnerships, strong and accountable institutions, scientific cooperation and regional policies that combine economic opportunity with the protection of nature. It also means ensuring that the communities and organisations caring for these landscapes have a voice in the decisions shaping their future.

Albania is not simply on its way to Europe. Ecologically, it has always been at its heart. Albania Is Biodiversity. And Albania’s biodiversity is a European responsibility.

items.content_html:
For years, Germany’s wind energy success story has been the subject of worldwide admiration. Delegations from elsewhere in Europe, US states, and numerous emerging economies came to see for themselves, leaving inspired by our approach. Yet instead of looking back with pride and pressing ahead with determination, we were stricken by the fear of success and slowed the pace of development, continuing to rely on gas and oil from Russia as supposedly cheap energy sources. China seized this opportunity to copy the German model and become the market leader in wind technology. Thousands of jobs in our domestic wind industry were lost. Today, the gravity of this error is becoming clear.

With Russia’s war on Ukraine and the Zeitenwende, including in relation to dependence on Russian energy, the consequences of decelerating the energy transition have come back to haunt us. Had Germany pursued its path with more alacrity and consistency, industry and consumers would not have been so hard hit by the ever-rising energy prices caused primarily by a distorted energy import market. Added to this are high tax burdens, which have made the conversion of wind power into stored energy, hydrogen, or synthetic, emission-free fuels uneconomical. But it is by no means too late to turn this situation around. In just a few years, we can establish a totally new basis for our economy.
I recall the year 2020, when, as a member of the Schleswig-Holstein state government and after a long struggle, I was able to secure the designation of two per cent of the state’s land area as priority zones for wind energy. This laid the foundation that enabled Tobias Goldschmidt, my successor as minister for the energy transition, to announce in August this year that the target of 10 gigawatts of onshore wind energy generation capacity had been achieved. This alone represents half of the output of the entire nuclear power sector in Germany at its peak. Wind energy is now the most important source of electricity in Germany. Twenty years ago, this would have been unthinkable.

While the myth of the “expensive energy transition” is currently being peddled, this could not be further from the truth. According to surveys by the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (ISE), wind energy – at five to 10 cents per kilowatt-hour – is by far the cheapest form of electricity generation after ground-mounted photovoltaics. Even modern gas-fired power stations incur costs that are almost twice as high, not to mention the production costs of nuclear power, which are many times higher, without even taking into account increasing shortfalls in output due to climate-related shutdowns. The truth is that wind energy is our strongest safeguard against the “hidden” cost drivers that are increasingly becoming visible.

While wind energy has the potential to create jobs and generate added value in many parts of Germany and Europe more broadly, in addition to guaranteeing an affordable supply of electricity, our dependence on conventional energy sources poses an ever-growing threat to security and prosperity. The war in Iran, with the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, has brought home once again how vulnerable we are to supply bottlenecks and price fluctuations. What’s more, the consumption of gas and oil on the world market inevitably leads to additional income for Putin’s Russia, which still exports large quantities of these commodities as well as a significant proportion of the world’s uranium, allowing it to finance what is now the fifth year of its war against Ukraine.

As the scorching summer of 2026 draws to a close, the immense economic burden caused by rapidly advancing climate change is also becoming apparent. The economy recorded losses of hundreds of millions of euros in June and July alone, not to speak of massive healthcare costs and the many heat-related deaths, which defy quantification and are, above all, a terrible human loss. The scale of municipal investment required for heat resilience measures is becoming clear. Alongside defence, infrastructure renewal, and industrial transformation, this represents the next major strain on public finances. It has become abundantly clear that Germany’s most important source of electricity – wind power – is its most effective safeguard against these ever-rising costs and represents a huge opportunity for Germany and Europe to place their industrial and technological base on a solid footing for the long term.

This text was translated by Katy Nicholson.

I keep returning to the same problem: where queer life is policed, the archive is not only missing – it is made missing. What survives often does so as residue. A rumor hardens into a route. A screenshot becomes evidence. A voice note is saved “just in case.” 

I write from interviews and materials circulating between people: chat logs, press fragments, scanned pages, and remembered locations. Some identifying details have been withheld or changed for safety. In Baku, the archive rarely appears as a stable collection. It appears as a sequence of ruptures – sudden drops in safety, visibility, and language – after which people reorganize their lives. This is not a complete chronology, but an attempt to name repeated interruption.

Rupture I – 2017: The Raid as a Method

In September 2017, Azerbaijani police detained more than 80 people in Baku, primarily men perceived as gay or bisexual, and transgender women. Testimonies describe beatings, humiliation, forced medical examinations, extortion, and pressure to identify others. Authorities presented the operation as an anti-prostitution campaign, a justification challenged by human-rights organizations.

In collective memory, 2017 is not only a year but a technique: the moment the state demonstrated what could happen to already vulnerable bodies. Phones were searched and contacts extracted. People remember the last message before leaving home, missed calls through the night, and the first message afterward: “I’m alive.” The raid targeted bodies, but also the networks inside their phones.

Rupture II – Codes, Class, and the Uneven Map

After a raid, gatherings do not disappear; they change their grammar. Interviews describe fewer direct invitations and more coded recognition, checking, and triangulation through friends. Public space remains, but becomes harder to read.

This difficulty is unevenly distributed. People with private apartments, encrypted platforms, or transnational networks adapt differently from those embedded in family and local surveillance. One young person outside Baku exchanged intimate messages online. When someone accessed the phone, the conversation moved into family space and became a threat. Repression required no uniform: it operated domestically, communally, and logistically. Queer public space is never only public; it is threaded through homes, schools, and screens.

Rupture III – Trans Presence and Structural Neglect

Trans lives often enter archives as scandals, footnotes, or absences. In 2020, Aysu Mammadli, a 28-year-old trans woman, was murdered in Baku, with other trans women surviving serious attacks. In one case, a woman who had been repeatedly stabbed was initially turned away from a state hospital and treated with hostility [4, 5].

Gender policing exposes trans people disproportionately, while the conditions necessary for documentation – safety, time, institutional shelter – are unevenly distributed. The archive does not exclude trans lives by accident. Sometimes the only record of an assault is a message sent afterward; the only proof that a friend existed – a saved contact; the only witness – a group chat that goes silent.

Rupture IV – Leaving and the Loss of Witnesses

Migration appears repeatedly as a survival strategy. Interviews describe routes through Istanbul, Tbilisi, Brussels, and Madrid, and friends who arrived first with advice or warnings. Leaving can reduce immediate danger, but it also removes witnesses. When people who documented, advocated, and translated events leave, the public record thins.

The 2022 murder of queer journalist and activist Avaz Hafizli was not only a personal loss but an infrastructural one. He recorded, verified, connected people, and published under pressure. In authoritarian conditions, public memory often depends on a few people carrying disproportionate risk. When they are removed, the archive becomes more fragile.

Rupture V – The Shrinking of Civic Oxygen

Interviews describe a narrowing environment: fewer independent platforms, higher costs for speaking out, and exhaustion alongside censorship. Beginning in 2023, authorities arrested journalists and staff from independent outlets including Abzas Media. In June 2025, seven Abzas Media journalists and media workers received prison sentences of seven to nine years in cases condemned as politically motivated.

The consequence is practical. Documentation becomes dependent on informal circulation. Screenshots and messages serve as public documents because formal records are absent or distrusted.

Rupture VI – Weaponized Intimacy

Intimacy is infrastructure. Desire creates routes, meeting points, and informal systems of safety. But it can also be converted into evidence. Screenshots, chats, photographs, and voice notes are kept because memory is fragile and proof may matter; the same materials can be used for blackmail, coercion, outing, or public humiliation.

Governance does not need to ban desire. It can control the conditions under which desire travels. When sex work appears here, it must be understood as a socioeconomic condition rather than a moral category. An archive must record these arrangements without exposing or punishing the people who lived them.

Rupture VII – 27 December 2025: The Raid Returns

Shortly after midnight on 27 December 2025, police raided a queer-friendly venue in central Baku and detained at least 106 people. Witnesses reported violence, degrading treatment, threats, phone searches, and coerced payments.

What is striking is not only the scale but the familiarity. The raid returns as a method, converting a semi-public space into exposure and showing how quickly brief normality can become a trap. Once again, the archive formed immediately, not as an official record but as a counter-record assembled from posts, testimony, and shared evidence. The raid tested documentation itself: what could be recorded, what had to remain hidden, and who would carry the risk of speaking.

What Can an Activist Archive Do Before the Next Rupture?

An activist archive cannot promise completeness or absolute safety. It can, however, minimize harm. Where visibility may trigger retaliation, the first obligation is not exposure but survivability: preserving memory without increasing danger.

This means collecting only what is necessary, making consent ongoing and revocable, and allowing people to decide whether materials should be public, restricted, delayed, or destroyed. Identifying details can be separated from narratives; names, dates, and locations withheld; testimonies stored under pseudonyms or sealed for later release. Access can be tiered, sensitive files encrypted, and custodianship shared rather than concentrated in one vulnerable person or institution. No storage method is automatically safe; each archive requires an assessment of who might seek access, what disclosure could cause, and where materials can be held most securely.

Counter-archiving is not merely a collection but a practice of protection. Repression interrupts documentation, but it does not end it. Memory changes form, moves between custodians, and finds quieter routes. What cannot be spoken openly today may still be preserved for tomorrow. What survives may not always be visible, but it remains. And in remaining, it creates the possibility that future readers will encounter not silence, but trace.
items.title: Azerbaijan: Seven Ruptures Shape Queer Life and Memory in Baku Analysis Queer life in Azerbaijan has been repeatedly disrupted by police raids, public intimidation, and the erosion of spaces where intimacy and community can exist. This article follows seven “ruptures” shaping how queer lives are lived and remembered in Baku. Yazgul Umar

Shortly after receiving your application, our Volunteer Team will invite candidates to a friendly Meet and Greet session. Selected volunteers will then be notified of their role, department, and invited to a Volunteer Orientation ahead of the festival.

What does it take to move from ambition on gender integration to everyday practice? For peacebuilding organisations, this is not only a question of programmes. It is also about how we organise ourselves. The systems, processes, conversations and ways of working within our organisations can enable gender-responsive practice across different contexts.

It is this organisational dimension of gender integration that PeaceNexus and its partners have been exploring together over the past five years. We have been hosting a peer-learning group on gender integration since 2021, following a series of round-tables hosted with Conciliation Resources and CMI – Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation. In 2023, four small grants were also awarded to four organisations ready to strengthen gender integration within. Their entry points were different but their challenges were shared: a gap between awareness and application, uneven engagement across teams, difficulty translating tools into practice and challenges in sustaining progress over time. Dedicated efforts towards achieving greater internal alignment led to progress and new pathways of change. We are proud to be publishing today this Reflection Paper, in partnership with our four partners: the Berghof Institute, Saferworld, CMI-Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation and Peaceful Change Initiative, as well as the larger peer-learning group.

Read the full paper here: Gender-Integration-Reflection-Paper.pdf
items.title: New Reflection Paper: Operationalising Gender Integration in Peacebuilding Organisations
items.summary:
What does it take to move from ambition on gender integration to everyday practice? For peacebuilding organisations, this is not only a question of programmes. It is also about how we organise ourselves. The systems, processes, conversations and ways of working within our organisations can enable gender-responsive practice across different contexts.

It is this organisational dimension of gender integration that PeaceNexus and its partners have been exploring together over the past five years. We have been hosting a peer-learning group on gender integration since 2021, following a series of round-tables hosted with Conciliation Resources and CMI – Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation. In 2023, four small grants were also awarded to four organisations ready to strengthen gender integration within. Their entry points were different but their challenges were shared: a gap between awareness and application, uneven engagement across teams, difficulty translating tools into practice and challenges in sustaining progress over time. Dedicated efforts towards achieving greater internal alignment led to progress and new pathways of change. We are proud to be publishing today this Reflection Paper, in partnership with our four partners: the Berghof Institute, Saferworld, CMI-Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation and Peaceful Change Initiative, as well as the larger peer-learning group.

Read the full paper here: Gender-Integration-Reflection-Paper.pdf

In Nairobi's informal settlements, seeking health care can mean bracing for judgment before you've even described your symptoms.

A queer, masculine-presenting woman walks into a clinic. The nurse looks up before asking anything about her health. “Are you a boy? Why are you dressed like that?”

She leaves without care.

A teenager comes in to ask about contraception. She’s sexually active and wants to protect herself. The nurse delivers the verdict before hearing anything else: “You are too young to be here for this. Go home and stop having sex.”

She leaves without care too, and without the assistance that could have kept her from becoming a teenage mother.

These aren't hypothetical scenarios. They're accounts shared directly by our grantee partner in Nairobi, describing what happens inside the clinics they're working to change.

This is what happens when a clinic has already decided who deserves care and who doesn’t. And when access becomes humiliating enough, people stop trying. They manage unwanted pregnancies alone. They seek abortions unsafely. They decide that showing up costs more than staying home.

September 28 is International Safe Abortion Day. This year's call is for solidarity in action. Safe abortion is healthcare, and protecting it means standing with the people and systems that provide it. That solidarity matters more than ever: in May 2026, Kenya's Court of Appeal struck down a ruling that had affirmed the right to abortion. According to the Center for Reproductive Rights, at least 2,600 women die from unsafe abortion in Kenya every year. Decisions like this one deepen that risk, and make long-term investment in partners like this one more urgent, not less.

What does a safe space look like? It's where a girl who has survived sexual violence can say what happened without being judged. Where a young woman can ask about contraception without being told she's too young. Where a gender non-conforming person can make decisions about their own body.

Our grantee partner in Nairobi is working to build just that. Several of the women leading this work know exactly what’s at stake because they’ve lived it — survivors of unsafe abortions themselves, turned away by the very clinics meant to help them.

Now they are bringing together queer people, sex workers, parents, pastors, chiefs, county officials, and healthcare workers one uncomfortable conversation at a time. Sex and abortion used to be taboo to discuss publicly in these communities. But when girls as young as seven have experienced sexual abuse, these conversations are crucial to ensure that young girls and women have the information to make decisions about their own bodies.
The results of these conversations are real: teenage pregnancies have dropped. Pastors who once preached against abortion have changed their minds. Elected officials have shown up to meetings and pushed for change in the county assembly.

But the work never ends. In Kenya, the government reassigns chiefs and health workers on a routine cycle, sometimes twice in a year. Every healthcare provider our partner trains can be replaced within months by someone with none of that training. The conversations must start over. The trust gets rebuilt from scratch.

"We are fighting against the anti-rights movement," one grantee told us. Opponents of abortion and queer rights rarely call themselves that; they speak the language of "family values" instead — a respectable-sounding cover. What they have that our partner doesn't is unrestricted money and no expiration date on their funding.

Most grants come with a deadline: prove it worked within a year or two, or the funding stops. But shifting how a community thinks doesn’t happen on that schedule because behavior change doesn't happen on a schedule. That's the gap our flexible, long-term, trust-based funding is built to close.

items.content_html:
Hunting for resources - are the countries of the Western Balkans experiencing a wave of colonisation?

Recording of the panel discussion, 13th May 2024.

With the Critical Raw Material Act (CRMA), the EU wants to reduce dependence on China. This has already had devastating consequences in the Western Balkans: Western companies are mining valuable materials without any regard for nature. Local communities are warning against disregard for international environmental protection standards, and environmental activists are being threatened. Critics are talking about colonial exploitation. The panel discussion will examine the question of how credible green policies in Europe are when negative consequences such as environmental pollution are exported to poorer countries.
items.title: Critical Raw Materials in South Eastern Europe Dossier The Western Balkans have critical raw materials, such as lithium in Serbia. These are essential for the EU's green transition. But there are fears locally that democratization will be sold out, and massive protests are directed against environmental damage and corruption.

In March 2025, Namibia entered the history books when it swore in its first woman president, alongside a woman vice president, a woman speaker of parliament, its first woman Supreme Court justice, and filling eight ministerial portfolios with women; many of us felt the ground shift. For a young democracy, this is seismic. As a queer Namibian and feminist activist, I felt both pride and pause. Pride, because glass ceilings cracked. Pause, because representation does not necessarily mean transformation - especially if systems of injustice are still maintained by patriarchal means of governance. 

Representation Is Not the Revolution - Transformation Is

African feminist thought has long insisted that representation is a doorway, not the destination. Women in office matter. But the revolution is measured in policy, participation and protection.

Namibia’s first woman president, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, emerges from the ruling party SWAPO Party, which in 2014 introduced its landmark “zebra list” policy - a gender-parity mechanism requiring a 50/50 alternation of women and men on party candidate lists. It significantly increased women’s participation in the National Assembly, raising it to approximately 46 percent and positioning Namibia among the continent’s leaders in parliamentary gender parity. By 2025, such policies helped Namibia make history as the first country in the world with women holding its top three leadership positions. Yet beyond these remarkable milestones of representation, substantive equality remains uneven.

Representation has shifted; structural vulnerability endures.

In Namibia, structural inequality persists despite advances in political representation. The raw gender pay gap indicates that women earn approximately 11 - 14 percent less than men on an hourly basis. Gender-based violence (GBV) remains endemic: an estimated 33 percent of women aged 15 - 49 have experienced physical, sexual, or emotional violence from an intimate partner. In 2024 alone, more than 5,000 cases of GBV were reported. A large number of cases, overall, reported in a single year for a country of just three million inhabitances. Civil society organisations have repeatedly called for GBV to be declared a national disaster. In 2020, a broad-based feminist campaign mobilized over 60,000 signatures - the largest petition effort of its kind - demanding the repeal of the restrictive 1975 Abortion and Sterilization Act, a law inherited from apartheid South Africa. Namibia finally gained independence from apartheid South Africa in 1990. Yet, despite women occupying the highest offices of the state, these longstanding civil rights demands have not translated into comprehensive legislative reform or systemic protection. Representation has shifted; structural vulnerability endures.

True transformation asks: Are patriarchal norms being dismantled? Are economic inequalities shrinking? Are women in rural areas, informal settlements, and care economies experiencing tangible change? And crucially, are LGBTQI+ Namibians safer, freer, and recognized under the law? 

Thus, we have come to understand the litmus test of women’s political leadership is not numerical parity - it is whether power is exercised to expand dignity for all.

The “Born-Free Feminist Paradox”

I am part of Namibia’s born-free generation - raised after apartheid and promised equality under one of Africa’s most progressive constitutions. Yet for many queer youth like myself, our coming of age has unfolded at a painful crossroads: growing up in a liberated democracy while colonial-era laws continued to criminalize our existence. Before independence, our parents were denied dignity and the right to love freely because of the color of their skin. More than three decades later, LGBTQI+ Namibians remained bound by the shackles of apartheid-era sodomy laws, relegated to second-class citizenship. How “born-free” are we, truly, if freedom is still conditional?

In June 2023, Namibia’s Supreme Court recognized same-sex marriages lawfully concluded abroad between a Namibian and a foreign spouse, affirming that queer Namibians are “part and parcel of the fabric of our society.” In 2024, the Windhoek High Court struck down the apartheid-era sodomy offence, reinforcing constitutional protections of dignity and equality. These were landmark affirmations of constitutional democracy.

Yet progress in the courts was met with backlash in parliament. Regressive unconstitutional legislation targeting LGBTQI+ recognition followed, accompanied by political rhetoric that blurred the line between moral panic and statecraft. Words matter. When leaders tasked with upholding the rule of law frame queer equality as a threat, it reverberates beyond parliamentary chambers. The youth-led civil rights movement, Equal Namibia, documented a surge in hostility and violence following the passage of these anti-LGBTQI+ bills, and seven members of our community lost their lives in the shadow of this polarized moment. 

State-sanctioned homophobia stands in tension with the very ethos of anti-colonial freedom.

This is the paradox: a liberation movement that fought racial oppression now presides over laws that marginalize queer citizens. President Nandi-Ndaitwah is herself a veteran of the liberation struggle. That legacy carries moral authority. But liberation cannot be selective. State-sanctioned homophobia stands in tension with the very ethos of anti-colonial freedom SWAPO once championed.

The question before Namibia is not whether women can lead - they demonstrably can. It is whether leadership born from liberation will extend freedom in full; especially with gender parity in parliament.

Namibia: 4th Most Tolerant in Africa - But Elite Politics Lag Behind

Afrobarometer ranks Namibia among the more socially tolerant countries on the continent, with 51 percent of Namibians tolerant towards those in same-sex relationships. Ordinary Namibians often display more openness than political rhetoric suggests. Yet elite politics has increasingly leaned toward populist moralism. Namibians are not “homophobic”; or opposed to “sexual and reproductive rights” - our politicians are. And this is where transformation is needed; not just representation. 

Ordinary Namibians often display more openness than political rhetoric suggests.

Civil society sees both opportunity and contradiction. We celebrate women’s ascent while recognizing that formal equality does not automatically yield feminist governance. If this administration truly wishes to pioneer gender equality, it must align representation with rights: protect civic space, affirm bodily autonomy, and resist anti-rights mobilizations that target women and queer communities alike.

Namibia stands at a defining moment. The world is watching a country led by women. We are proud of our women in leadership. The deeper question is whether this leadership will widen democracy or merely symbolize it.

Representation opened the door. Transformation - especially in how LGBTQI+ and sexual and reproductive rights are treated - will determine whether this historic moment becomes a feminist milestone or a missed opportunity.

The country stands at a crossroads between symbolic progress and true transformation. Omar van Reenen

Published on 3 July 2026

On 27 September 2026 the Swiss electorate will vote on the Neutrality Initiative. The central question is whether we wish to retain neutrality in its current form, or whether an article should be inserted into the Federal Constitution requiring a stricter practice of neutrality. The latter would mark a clear change of direction. Neutrality has been enshrined in the Federal Constitution since 1848. The outcome of the vote does not call Switzerland’s neutrality into question. The point is how it should be applied in future.

Switzerland’s neutrality has been enshrined in the Federal Constitution since 1848. It is internationally recognised and safeguarded under international law. Switzerland uses its neutrality to protect its security, independence and prosperity. Neutrality contributes to Switzerland’s ability to provide its good offices.

Aim of the Neutrality Initiative

The initiative calls for the stricter practice of neutrality and seeks to add a new article to the Federal Constitution stating that:

  • Switzerland’s neutrality shall be perpetual and armed;
  • Switzerland shall not join any military or defence alliance, neither shall it cooperate with such an alliance, unless Switzerland is under military attack or such an attack is being prepared;
  • Switzerland shall not take part in armed conflicts between third countries and shall not impose sanctions against warring parties. Exceptions are made for sanctions decided by the United Nations (UN) and measures to prevent the circumvention of sanctions; and
  • Switzerland uses its neutrality to fulfil its role as mediator.

neutralitaet-ja.ch

Position of the Federal Council and Parliament

The Federal Council and Parliament reject the Neutrality Initiative without offering a counter-proposal. In their essence, the demands of the initiative correspond to the legal obligations of a neutral state, which Switzerland already upholds in practice.

  • Switzerland is permanently neutral, therefore its neutrality is already perpetual.
  • It is current practice that, as a permanently neutral state, Switzerland does not join any military or defence alliance such as NATO.
  • Under the present system Switzerland does not take part in armed conflicts between third countries.
  • Switzerland already adopts all UN sanctions. As a member of the UN it is required to do so.
  • The initiative committee is calling for Switzerland to use its neutrality in its role as mediator and to promote peace. That is already the current practice.

Where the demands of the initiative exceed what is the practice today, they damage Switzerland's interests:

  • Compared with current practice the initiative would curtail the flexibility that allows Switzerland to protect its security, independence and prosperity. This room for manoeuvre is particularly important amid a deteriorating security situation.
  • The initiative would impede cooperation on security policy. Switzerland cannot wait until it is attacked to begin cooperating, as the initiative envisages, as this would have grave consequences for the country's security. Switzerland would be excluded from knowledge-sharing, cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy, and be less secure in the event of an attack.
  • Sanctions are a means of responding to violations of international law and threats to the international order. As a small state, Switzerland benefits especially from this order. Under the initiative Switzerland would no longer be able to adopt sanctions against warring states, which would impact on both it’s interests and reputation. In certain cases it might also trigger a backlash from other states.

Neutrality Initiative: without counter-proposal, the Federal Council recommends rejection (Federal Council press release, 26.6.2024)

Dispatch on the popular initiative ‘Safeguarding Swiss Neutrality (Neutrality Initiative)’ (de)

Parliamentary debate 24.092 ‘Safeguarding Swiss neutrality (Neutrality Initiative)’, popular initiative (Curia Vista)

FAQ

Sanctions

  • Where sanctions are decided by the UN, as a member State Switzerland is bound to adopt them.

    The Embargo Act provides the legal foundation for adopting sanctions outside the UN. On this basis, the Federal Council decides on a case-by-case basis whether adopting the sanctions is in Switzerland’s interests. It may adopt sanctions imposed by the EU, the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) or Switzerland’s main trading partners in full, in part or in an amended form. Following Russia’s illegal attack on Ukraine, the Federal Council decided to adopt most of the EU’s sanctions against Russia.

    When adopting sanctions Switzerland’s neutrality is relevant only if those sanctions concern goods that directly affect the military strength of a warring party. These are referred to as ‘militarily relevant goods’. If Switzerland restricts the export or transit of such goods for one warring party, it must apply the same restrictions to the other warring party, as required by the law of neutrality.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Sanctions

      PDF103.79 kB8 July 2026

  • States may respond with sanctions if other states violate international law. Recent years have seen an increase in sanctions imposed outside the UN framework. One of the reasons is that major powers are often unable to agree, so the UN Security Council sometimes cannot reach a decision. Outside the UN, states or regional organisations such as the EU may decide to impose sanctions. For example, the EU imposed sanctions against Russia in response to the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine. Even if they were not decided by the UN, adopting such sanctions is consistent with Switzerland’s neutrality.

    When Switzerland joins broadly supported sanctions – particularly in the event of a war of aggression against another State – its actions help to strengthen peace and a just international order. That is in Switzerland's own interest.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Sanctions

      PDF103.79 kB8 July 2026

Good offices

  • Good offices can help to de-escalate or resolve conflicts between states or within an individual state. In some cases they also serve to maintain dialogue between conflict parties, and to mitigate the consequences of armed conflict.

    Switzerland has a long tradition of good offices, and they are an important component of its foreign policy. They represent values that are associated with the state, such as reliability, discretion, rigour and impartiality.

    Neutrality is not a precondition for the ability to mediate credibly. However, alongside a Swiss political system built on dialogue, a willingness to compromise and cultural diversity, and characteristics such as discretion, expertise and flexibility, neutrality can reinforce trust in Switzerland and improve its credibility as a mediator.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Good Offices

      PDF113.18 kB8 July 2026

Exports of war materiel

  • Under the law of neutrality Switzerland is prohibited from supplying any material relevant for war purposes directly to parties to conflict from its own military inventory. In the case of private-sector exports Switzerland must treat all warring parties equally.  This means that if Switzerland restricts exports from private-sector entities to one party to a conflict, it must apply the same restrictions to the other party, as required by the principle of equal treatment.

    The War Materiel Act also applies. This goes beyond the law of neutrality. The War Materiel Act provides that export licences for war materiel will not be granted if the destination state is involved in international or non-international armed conflict. It applies equally to military inventory and private-sector entities.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and the export of war material

      PDF152.83 kB16 July 2026

  • The Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA) authorises overflights by foreign military and other state aircraft. Requests of major political importance, especially those concerning permits for flights relating to preparations or support for hostilities, are referred by the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DETEC) to the Federal Council for decision. The Ordinance on the Protection of Airspace Sovereignty is the authoritative basis here.

    Decisions on arms exports must be made in accordance with the relevant legal foundations, specifically the Federal Act on War Materiel and the Goods Control Act. Here, too, the Federal Council decides on requests of major foreign or security policy importance.

    Neutrality is always taken into account when a decision is made.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and the export of war material

      PDF152.83 kB16 July 2026

  • Neutrality may for example also be a factor in the export of so-called as dual-use goods (i.e. those that can be used for both civilian and military purposes) and specific military goods (designed specifically for military purposes, but not classified as weapons or ammunition themselves; e.g. body armour). Their export to a country at war might also constitute the grant of military advantage, so the neutrality plays a role here too.

    Neutrality may also be of relevance in connection with private security services provided abroad. These services which fall under the Federal Act on Private Security Services Provided Abroad must be reviewed to ensure their consistency with neutrality. The services must be prohibited if they provide a militarily advantage to one party to a conflict.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and the export of war material

      PDF152.83 kB16 July 2026

Neutrality and security policy

  • Switzerland is subject to cross-border threats in just the same way as other European states. The security policy climate has become more uncertain and will remain unstable in the future. It is therefore in Switzerland's interest to align its security and defence policy with international cooperation.

    As a neutral state Switzerland is permitted to take part in international military exercises of a war context. Participation in such exercises does not come with any obligations of joint defence. These exercises allow Switzerland to enhance its own capabilities in comparison with foreign armed forces. If Switzerland were attacked, it would be able to cooperate with other states to defend itself. However, such cooperation cannot be practiced for only in an emergency, but must rather be trained for in advance.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Security Policy

      PDF141.89 kB8 July 2026

Switzerland’s neutrality

items.title: More about «Neutrality Initiative»
items.summary:
Published on 3 July 2026

On 27 September 2026 the Swiss electorate will vote on the Neutrality Initiative. The central question is whether we wish to retain neutrality in its current form, or whether an article should be inserted into the Federal Constitution requiring a stricter practice of neutrality. The latter would mark a clear change of direction. Neutrality has been enshrined in the Federal Constitution since 1848. The outcome of the vote does not call Switzerland’s neutrality into question. The point is how it should be applied in future.

Switzerland’s neutrality has been enshrined in the Federal Constitution since 1848. It is internationally recognised and safeguarded under international law. Switzerland uses its neutrality to protect its security, independence and prosperity. Neutrality contributes to Switzerland’s ability to provide its good offices.

Aim of the Neutrality Initiative

The initiative calls for the stricter practice of neutrality and seeks to add a new article to the Federal Constitution stating that:

  • Switzerland’s neutrality shall be perpetual and armed;
  • Switzerland shall not join any military or defence alliance, neither shall it cooperate with such an alliance, unless Switzerland is under military attack or such an attack is being prepared;
  • Switzerland shall not take part in armed conflicts between third countries and shall not impose sanctions against warring parties. Exceptions are made for sanctions decided by the United Nations (UN) and measures to prevent the circumvention of sanctions; and
  • Switzerland uses its neutrality to fulfil its role as mediator.

neutralitaet-ja.ch

Position of the Federal Council and Parliament

The Federal Council and Parliament reject the Neutrality Initiative without offering a counter-proposal. In their essence, the demands of the initiative correspond to the legal obligations of a neutral state, which Switzerland already upholds in practice.

  • Switzerland is permanently neutral, therefore its neutrality is already perpetual.
  • It is current practice that, as a permanently neutral state, Switzerland does not join any military or defence alliance such as NATO.
  • Under the present system Switzerland does not take part in armed conflicts between third countries.
  • Switzerland already adopts all UN sanctions. As a member of the UN it is required to do so.
  • The initiative committee is calling for Switzerland to use its neutrality in its role as mediator and to promote peace. That is already the current practice.

Where the demands of the initiative exceed what is the practice today, they damage Switzerland's interests:

  • Compared with current practice the initiative would curtail the flexibility that allows Switzerland to protect its security, independence and prosperity. This room for manoeuvre is particularly important amid a deteriorating security situation.
  • The initiative would impede cooperation on security policy. Switzerland cannot wait until it is attacked to begin cooperating, as the initiative envisages, as this would have grave consequences for the country's security. Switzerland would be excluded from knowledge-sharing, cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy, and be less secure in the event of an attack.
  • Sanctions are a means of responding to violations of international law and threats to the international order. As a small state, Switzerland benefits especially from this order. Under the initiative Switzerland would no longer be able to adopt sanctions against warring states, which would impact on both it’s interests and reputation. In certain cases it might also trigger a backlash from other states.

Neutrality Initiative: without counter-proposal, the Federal Council recommends rejection (Federal Council press release, 26.6.2024)

Dispatch on the popular initiative ‘Safeguarding Swiss Neutrality (Neutrality Initiative)’ (de)

Parliamentary debate 24.092 ‘Safeguarding Swiss neutrality (Neutrality Initiative)’, popular initiative (Curia Vista)

Sanctions

  • Where sanctions are decided by the UN, as a member State Switzerland is bound to adopt them.

    The Embargo Act provides the legal foundation for adopting sanctions outside the UN. On this basis, the Federal Council decides on a case-by-case basis whether adopting the sanctions is in Switzerland’s interests. It may adopt sanctions imposed by the EU, the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) or Switzerland’s main trading partners in full, in part or in an amended form. Following Russia’s illegal attack on Ukraine, the Federal Council decided to adopt most of the EU’s sanctions against Russia.

    When adopting sanctions Switzerland’s neutrality is relevant only if those sanctions concern goods that directly affect the military strength of a warring party. These are referred to as ‘militarily relevant goods’. If Switzerland restricts the export or transit of such goods for one warring party, it must apply the same restrictions to the other warring party, as required by the law of neutrality.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Sanctions

      PDF103.79 kB8 July 2026

  • States may respond with sanctions if other states violate international law. Recent years have seen an increase in sanctions imposed outside the UN framework. One of the reasons is that major powers are often unable to agree, so the UN Security Council sometimes cannot reach a decision. Outside the UN, states or regional organisations such as the EU may decide to impose sanctions. For example, the EU imposed sanctions against Russia in response to the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine. Even if they were not decided by the UN, adopting such sanctions is consistent with Switzerland’s neutrality.

    When Switzerland joins broadly supported sanctions – particularly in the event of a war of aggression against another State – its actions help to strengthen peace and a just international order. That is in Switzerland's own interest.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Sanctions

      PDF103.79 kB8 July 2026

  • Good offices can help to de-escalate or resolve conflicts between states or within an individual state. In some cases they also serve to maintain dialogue between conflict parties, and to mitigate the consequences of armed conflict.

    Switzerland has a long tradition of good offices, and they are an important component of its foreign policy. They represent values that are associated with the state, such as reliability, discretion, rigour and impartiality.

    Neutrality is not a precondition for the ability to mediate credibly. However, alongside a Swiss political system built on dialogue, a willingness to compromise and cultural diversity, and characteristics such as discretion, expertise and flexibility, neutrality can reinforce trust in Switzerland and improve its credibility as a mediator.

      PDF113.18 kB8 July 2026

    The War Materiel Act also applies. This goes beyond the law of neutrality. It applies equally to military inventory and private-sector entities.

      PDF152.83 kB16 July 2026
