items.content_html:
Funding is political.

Who decides where resources go matters, and, too often, funding decisions are made far from the communities most impacted by injustice. Participatory grantmaking challenges this approach by shifting decision-making closer to the people leading change.

Our new report, Participatory Grantmaking with Feminist Movements: Reflections on Power and Practice, reflects on five years of Global Fund for Women's experience supporting feminist movements with participatory grantmaking, and what we learned along the way.

The report explores how participatory grantmaking can strengthen movements, expand access to funding for historically under-resourced groups, and deepen trust. It also surfaces the tensions, tradeoffs, and complexities that come with shifting power via participatory grantmaking.

As movements continue organizing for justice under increasingly difficult conditions, philanthropy must also evolve, trusting movements not only to lead change, but to shape how resources flow and how success is defined.

Whether you are a funder, movement leader, researcher, or advocate, this report offers practical insights into building more equitable partnerships with movements driving change.

AMMAN, JORDAN – 10 SEPTEMBER 2026 

Representatives from the Greater Amman Municipality, the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, and Community Jameel inaugurated today a new tactical urbanism project along Al-Taj Street in Amman’s Al-Yarmouk District. The pilot project demonstrates how rapid, low-cost urban transformations can protect residents from extreme heat while creating safer, more welcoming spaces for children, students, and local families.

The Al-Taj Street pilot forms part of the work by the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, a partnership between C40 Cities and Community Jameel, which works directly with the cities of Amman and Chennai to align their spatial plans and land-use policies with climate targets, emissions pathways and climate risk data to deliver more sustainable, people-centred urban environments. The Labs have helped shape 15 urban planning policies, regulations and municipal strategies. In total, these policy and planning initiatives directly reach 4.5 million people, including 2.52 million climate-vulnerable residents across Amman.

Tactical urbanism uses short-term, low-cost, and scalable interventions to test long-term spatial change. Data collected through monitoring and evaluation of the site following the pilot’s inauguration will be analysed to inform future neighbourhood upgrading projects across Amman.

Delivered through the Jameel C40 Labs, the pilot reimagines two vulnerable sites along the congested Al-Taj Street corridor. By targeting a major school crossing for four schools and a central traffic island, the project turns key stretches of exposed asphalt into shaded, community-centred-public space.

Co-designed directly with local residents, the transformation delivers immediate climate solutions alongside vital community benefits: 

  • A cooler, safer school zone: Bright, heat-reflective street art now transforms dark asphalt at school gates, lowering surface temperatures while slowing traffic to protect students on their journey to and from school.

  • Shaded waiting and social spaces: New shade canopies, climbing green trellises, and native drought-tolerant planters offer cool, comfortable resting spots for residents.

  • Safe spaces for play: Children in the neighbourhood now have a dedicated, 250m2 play area placed safely away from heavy traffic, featuring custom climbing structures built from recycled materials.

  • Community pride and stewardship: Over 100m2 of vibrant wall murals were painted by local youth and volunteer groups, fostering the long-term community stewardship essential for sustained urban transformation.

Ahmad Al-Malkawi, Chairman of the Greater Amman Municipality Committee, said: "The Al-Taj Street project represents a pivotal opportunity to translate urban planning and design principles from a theoretical framework into tangible solutions that respond to the daily needs of residents. This tactical urbanism intervention provides a scalable and replicable model for neighbourhoods across Amman, particularly those most vulnerable to climate impacts. 

Through this participatory approach, we look forward to developing a more resilient, sustainable, and safe urban environment, while fostering accessible, inclusive, and welcoming public spaces in close collaboration with our international partners and the local community.”

George Richards, Director of Community Jameel, said: "Drawing on traditional urbanism practices in the Arab world as well as research and evidence-based design, the Al-Taj Street pilot shows how climate planning can move from strategy into implementation, creating accessible, climate-resilient public spaces for residents. Working closely with Greater Amman Municipality, the Jameel C40 Labs have helped align Amman’s urban planning policies with climate targets, emissions pathways and climate risk data to deliver more sustainable, people-centred neighbourhoods in the city."

Mark Watts, Executive Director of C40 Cities, said: "Great urban planning isn't just drawn on paper; it's tested on the streets alongside the people who live there. By combining a deeply people-centred approach with tactical urbanism, the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs and Greater Amman Municipality are turning ambitious climate goals into tangible change along Al-Taj street in Al Yarmouk neighbourhood. This project demonstrates how quick, cost-effective interventions can transform asphalt and unshaded public space into vibrant, heat-resilient communities - offering a clear blueprint not just for other neighborhoods across Amman, but for cities across the region."

The Al-Taj Street tactical urbanism project serves as a localised demonstration of the Jameel C40 Labs' broader policy and planning initiatives in Amman. Crucial to this wider effort is supporting the adoption of the Amman Zoning & Planning Bylaw in 2025, which represents a landmark shift for the city by formalising environmental considerations and community participation in urban planning for the very first time.

This legislative framework provides the foundation for neighbourhood-scale action. Building on this, the Jameel C40 Labs developed a climate-responsive neighbourhood plan for Kherbet Al-Souq - also known as Amman’s “Southern Gate” - a five-square-kilometre area expected to grow from around 25,000 residents today to 42,000 by 2050. In May 2026, the plan was formally handed over to the Greater Amman Municipality by the  Jameel C40 Labs, marking an important step in translating the Labs’ climate planning work into a practical framework for managing the neighbourhood’s growth and resilience. The plan focuses on measures including shaded and greener streets, safer walking routes, improved water management, accessible public spaces, climate-smart infrastructure and support for local livelihoods. 

The Al-Taj Street tactical urbanism project is a practical, localised demonstration of this broader neighbourhood approach, showing how climate-responsive planning principles can be translated into immediate, visible improvements while generating lessons that can inform implementation and future neighbourhood planning across Amman.

AMMAN, JORDAN – 9 SEPTEMBER 2026 

The Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, a partnership between C40 Cities and Community Jameel, together with Minecraft Education, the Greater Amman Municipality, and the Queen Rania Centre for Education and Information Technology, awarded  the winning prize of the Schools Reinventing Cities competition to Team Um Tufail from Um Tufail Mixed Secondary School at an official ceremony held today at the Al Hussein Cultural Centre in Amman. 

The competition brought together 97 students across 16 schools over a ten-week design challenge using the digital world of Minecraft Education, a game-based platform developed by the makers of Minecraft, the best-selling video game of all time, in which players use blocks to build and explore infinite worlds.

Through the competition, the students reimagined public spaces in the Al-Yadudah neighbourhood of Amman, with a focus on improving access to healthy food, tackling extreme heat, and creating vibrant, accessible places for play and community life. 

The competition forms part of the wider efforts of the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, which work directly with city authorities in Amman and Chennai to align spatial plans and land-use policies with climate targets, emissions pathways and climate risk data. Across both cities, the Labs have helped shape 15 urban planning policies, regulations, and municipal strategies, directly reaching 4.5 million people, including 2.52 million people in Amman.

Schools Reinventing Cities brings this climate planning work into the classroom, giving young people a role in reimagining the public spaces, systems, and climate-resilient neighbourhoods they envision for their city.

The awards ceremony brought together young innovators, city officials, urban planners, and educators to view the winning digital proposals. The teams were assessed based on the quality of their presentations, models, creativity, and the feasibility of implementing their proposals.

Team Um Tufail’s proposal addressed traffic congestion and air pollution, high energy use and waste, lack of green space, and overreliance on private cars in a rapidly growing city. The  proposal included a walkable neighbourhood with public transport, bicycle paths, and electric vehicle charging; solar energy and recycling; parks and natural areas; and connected community services such as a school, library, mosque, and shops. 

The jury found that Team Um Tufail envisioned “a community built around people, nature, and technology, where every area has a purpose and all areas work together as one connected system”. 

Team Eco Builders from Nusaybah Al-Maziniyah Mixed Secondary School came in second place, while the third place award went to Naifa AmmanCraft, from Naifeh First Secondary School for Girls, which presented a project titled Voxel.

The winning team stood out by integrating public transport into its neighbourhood design as a way to reduce emissions and dependence on private cars. The Team Um Tufail project will contribute to implementation of the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs’ plan for the wider Kherbet Al-Souq area, which was submitted to the Greater Amman Municipality in May 2026. 

The plan identifies public transport as critical to making its neighbourhoods, including Al-Yadudah, climate responsive, addressing urban sprawl, rising emissions, traffic congestion, and air pollution, while improving equitable access to jobs and services for lower-income households, women, and refugee populations.

Eng. Ziad Abu Arabi, Deputy City Manager for Planning and Economic Development at Greater Amman Municipality, said: “The initiative serves as a vital model for engaging youth in solving real urban and climate challenges, turning their creativity into visions for a greener, more resilient city.” He highlighted that collaboration with C40 Cities, Community Jameel, and local partners aligns Amman's efforts with global best practices, adding that “the initiative's true value lies in the practical skills and experience gained by the students.”

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes at Community Jameel, said: "Climate-resilient cities need to be shaped by the people who will live in them. Through the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, Community Jameel is pleased to support work that brings young people into the planning process, giving students in Amman a voice in reimagining safer, greener, and more inclusive neighbourhoods for the future.”

Eng. Muneeb Tashman, Director of the Queen Rania Center for Educational Technology and Information, Ministry of Education, highlighted: “the educational impact of applying Minecraft Education to real-world issues like transit, energy, water, and waste.” He noted that “the partnership reflects the integration of education with sustainable development, cultivating critical thinking, problem-solving, and teamwork among students” while commending the dedication of participating teachers and mentors.

Mark Watts, Executive Director of C40 Cities, said: "Young people are not just the future of our cities—they are ready to shape them right now. The ingenuity displayed by Amman’s youth in this year’s Schools Reinventing Cities challenge is nothing short of inspiring. By partnering with Community Jameel and Minecraft Education, C40 is proud to provide a platform that unleashes students' creativity, giving them a real voice in how their communities respond to the climate crisis. The ideas celebrated yesterday at the Al Hussein Cultural Centre prove that when students get a say in city building, they design cities that are not only climate-safe, but full of play, community, and possibility."

By proposing practical ways to improve public space, access to healthy food, and climate resilience, the Um Tufail students’ ideas will provide an additional youth perspective to the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs and Greater Amman Municipality’s ongoing planning and design process for Kherbet Al-Souq. Additional selected proposals will be shared with the Greater Amman Municipality to help inform future interventions as the neighbourhood develops.

items.content_html:
Ahead of the Berlin Climate and Security Conference, we explore what Germany should do to support the climate, peace, and security agenda.

Climate stress and conflict increasingly overlap. Climate stress does not automatically cause conflict. But where it interacts with weak governance, inequality, and existing instability, it can increase pressure on resources and deepen grievances.

Germany is actively advocating for more support for the climate-security nexus. Yet multiple questions remain around how it can best leverage its position to further advance this cause.

This was the subject of a roundtable on “Climate, peace, and security: Advancing Germany’s policy response”, co-organised with the International Rescue Committee Germany, at our office in Berlin in July. Leading stakeholders from politics, business, academia, and civil society discussed how Germany can more effectively embed climate-related security risks into its national security architecture as well as facilitate access to climate finance for conflict-affected countries.

Berghof’s Executive Director Chris Coulter said Germany “needed to align what already exists far more effectively.” She stressed that climate change is not simply a technical issue: it shapes dialogue and mediation and can also provide an entry point for negotiations.

Climate change is not simply a technical issue: it shapes dialogue and mediation and can also provide an entry point for negotiations.Chris Coulter, Executive Director

Connecting climate, peace, and security

For years, climate change and security have been treated as separate issues. Security discussions still follow a conventional military approach. The effects of climate change are not only felt in fragile and conflict-affected countries though but also on supply chains, energy prices, and food security, which have political consequences for Germany and Europe. This framing does not dilute Germany's responsibility or solidarity with the countries hit hardest. However, it makes preventive action politically legible to a wider audience.

The time has come for political leaders to treat climate risk as a core national security priority. A positive sign in this direction was registered at this year’s London Climate Week where climate and nature were framed as systemic risks.

Where the gaps remain

If climate is genuinely treated as a security threat, funding should follow. However, global aid budgets are shrinking. Even if programmes stop running, affected communities still must keep living with the consequences and adapt accordingly. This is compounded by the fact that countries most affected by climate change receive the least funding.

The broader collective-action problem around climate finance also raises a hard question of fairness: who gets left behind? And how do they get brought back into the conversation?

Germany’s policy response

Germany is already playing a leading role in connecting climate, peace, and security. Together with the island state of Nauru, Germany established the UN Group of Friends on Climate and Security with now over 70 Member States. It placed climate security within its Foreign and National Security Strategy and has an advisory commission drawing on civil society expertise, among others. Ahead of this year’s Berlin Climate and Security Conference, the priority should now be to connect existing policies, institutions, and expertise and turn them into practical action.

  • First, Germany should strengthen coordination across foreign policy, development, humanitarian action, climate, and security. Ministries and agencies need shared analysis and clearer objectives, particularly in fragile and conflict-affected countries.

  • Second, Germany should make climate action more conflict sensitive, while ensuring that peacebuilding and humanitarian programmes account for climate pressures. It should also connect high-level diplomacy and mediation more effectively with local authorities and communities.

  • Third, Germany should keep conflict prevention and climate adaptation at the centre of its response. As aid budgets shrink, funding decisions should protect anticipatory action and support communities already facing the combined effects of climate shocks, conflict, and weak governance.

Germany cannot advance this agenda alone. It should continue to work with the United Kingdom, France, and other European partners on shared analysis and coordinated diplomacy. The United Kingdom's new taskforce on nature, climate, and security offers one possible route for exchange. Closer European cooperation would also give Germany’s agenda greater weight in international forums at a time of geopolitical fragmentation and tighter budgets.

Finally, climate security must move beyond its usual policy circles. The case for it needs to be presented in the rooms where decisions on defence, trade, energy and critical minerals are made. Germany has helped build the climate, peace, and security agenda. Its next challenge is to turn that leadership into a joined-up policy that prevents conflict, supports communities, and treats climate resilience as part of security preparedness.

Germany is already playing a leading role in connecting climate, peace, and security. Together with the island state of Nauru, Germany established the UN Group of Friends on Climate and Security with now over 70 Member States. It placed climate security within its Foreign and National Security Strategy and has an advisory commission drawing on civil society expertise, among others. Ahead of this year’s Berlin Climate and Security Conference, the priority should now be to connect existing policies, institutions, and expertise and turn them into practical action.

  • First, Germany should strengthen coordination across foreign policy, development, humanitarian action, climate, and security. Ministries and agencies need shared analysis and clearer objectives, particularly in fragile and conflict-affected countries.

  • Second, Germany should make climate action more conflict sensitive, while ensuring that peacebuilding and humanitarian programmes account for climate pressures. It should also connect high-level diplomacy and mediation more effectively with local authorities and communities.

  • Third, Germany should keep conflict prevention and climate adaptation at the centre of its response. As aid budgets shrink, funding decisions should protect anticipatory action and support communities already facing the combined effects of climate shocks, conflict, and weak governance.

Germany cannot advance this agenda alone. It should continue to work with the United Kingdom, France, and other European partners on shared analysis and coordinated diplomacy. The United Kingdom's new taskforce on nature, climate, and security offers one possible route for exchange. Closer European cooperation would also give Germany’s agenda greater weight in international forums at a time of geopolitical fragmentation and tighter budgets.

Finally, climate security must move beyond its usual policy circles. The case for it needs to be presented in the rooms where decisions on defence, trade, energy and critical minerals are made. Germany has helped build the climate, peace, and security agenda. Its next challenge is to turn that leadership into a joined-up policy that prevents conflict, supports communities, and treats climate resilience as part of security preparedness.

items.content_html:
Séléty and Keur Ayib are two border villages close to Gambia have undergone rapid growth, making them among the most rapidly urbanising areas in Senegal. Both of these villages are located in the Senegambian cross-border area and are known for their cross-border dynamism. Though seemingly peripheral to Senegal’s main urban hubs, these border villages remain closely connected to Gambian towns - making them striking examples of the spatial and socio-economic shifts unfolding in the region.

Indeed, Senegalese rural areas on the border with Gambia are undergoing profound socio-spatial transformation, revealing merging urban dynamic. These shifts are driven by uneven development between town and countryside, eco-geographic disparities and economic potential, which are reshaping internal mobility of Senegalese people.

The Senegal-Gambia Border: A Pump for the Urbanisation of Rural Areas

The dynamics of urbanisation are underpinned by social and spatio-temporal factors: urbanisation can be seen as a phenomenon that transforms society's lifestyles. Over the last few decades, profound changes have occurred in certain Senegalese rural areas along the border with The Gambia, most evidently in the villages like Karang, Séléty and Keur Ayib along the border. This socio-spatial process of urbanisation can be measured in terms of population growth, socio-economic activities and spatial change.

Demographic growth in these villages has reached rates that defied all statistical projections. For example, between 1988 and 2010, the population of Keur Ayib rose from 782 to 4,0001. Beyond natural population growth, rising numbers are largely driven by positive net migration—clear evidence that rural Senegal is undergoing a process of urbanisation.   One effect of the demographic growth was observed by a former mayor of Médina-Sabakh, a commune of which Keur Ayib is one of the largest villages, who said: "Keur Ayib is suffocating and the demand for housing and services is growing by the day. Rapid urbanisation is a real phenomenon and suffers from a lack of planning"2.  

The physical landscape reveals a marked change in the built environment. Over the last few decades, housing has been modernised to keep pace with the arrival of newcomers and new sectors of profitable activity. Senegalese villages are increasingly being built on terraces and on high ground. The findings speak for themselves: 83% of those we surveyed for a study now live in modern housing, while 24% are in transitional dwellings - leaving just 17% in traditional structures.

The rise of modern housing, often built by emerging social classes and rented to civil servants, marks a visible shift in the local landscape. Open, communal living spaces are increasingly giving way to enclosed, individual compounds - a clear sign of an urbanising society where privacy, status, and property boundaries are becoming more prominent.

In addition to this, there is an exponential spread of occupied space. Villages and towns that were once far apart now form a continuum. This rapid and spontaneous occupation of space is creating disorder and insecurity, leading to planning problems.

Border dynamics are driving rural urbanisation in Senegal.

The urbanisation of rural areas in Senegal is essentially due to a crisis in the rural economy and the opportunities offered by secondary towns. Since their creation, the main activity ensuring development in these villages was agriculture. The rural economy, based on working the land and processing its products, occupied the majority of the inhabitants and enabled the farmers to guarantee food self-sufficiency. However, the rural economy suffered a real crisis with the drought of the 1970s and the subsequent deterioration in trade. The search for alternatives led rural dwellers to convert to the trade, craft, tourism and services sectors.

Among the factors that explain the urban dynamic are geographical position, the development of the road network and the low cost of land. Villages located on the border and near secondary towns have benefited from opportunities such as the existence of the road network and the accessibility to land, which have accelerated their urbanisation. The secondary towns have also experienced a demographic boom, accompanied by promiscuity, insecurity, a growing informal sector and a high demand for basic social services. The major consequences of this situation are the saturation of dedicated structures and infrastructure, the disappearance of traditional activities and land speculation, which is a source of conflict between locals and migrants.

Transit areas are the main places of attraction as the large numbers of people passing through these areas make trade and related activities very profitable. The new players need to transform this formerly agricultural space for their housing and the expansion of their activities.

Furthermore, increased consumption and the opportunity to travel to the rest of the country have encouraged the demographic explosion and socio-spatial changes in Senegalese villages located along the Senegal/Gambia border. Proximity to Gambian urban centres - along with differences in currency and cost of living - has fuelled strong ties between town and countryside. These cross-border dynamics are accelerating urbanisation in Senegal’s rural areas, where some villages now function as informal extensions of Gambian cities, serving as commuter hubs or dormitory towns for urban workers.

Political instability and economic hardship have also reshaped Senegal’s rural borderlands. Indeed, the coups d'état in The Gambia and the long-running conflict in the Casamance region are key drivers for migration. Many refugees took advantage of this to acquire land and settle permanently. Another less visible force behind this transformation is “Communitisation”. Communitisation refers to belonging to the same family or ethnic group on which the territory is built, which has led to the formation of socially homogenous neighbourhoods and reinforced local territorial identities3.

The Transformation of City Lifestyles 

The demographic boom, the diversity of business sectors and the presence of civil servants have all contributed to raising living standards. As a result, the landscape has been transformed by changes in housing, the densification and consumption of agricultural land, and the emergence of new lifestyles (food and clothing). The construction of major infrastructure and new housing and service facilities is helping to modernise the built environment in rural areas. With this in mind, the State of Senegal's "one family, one roof" social housing programme, which is being carried out in peri-urban areas, is contributing to the urbanisation of these rural areas. For instance, the planned development of 1,500 plots across 50 hectares in Keur Ayib, along with a five-hectare Customs House project set to include 300 homes, underscores the rapid urbanisation taking place in border areas.

Long waits at border crossings are doing more than slowing travellers - they’re fuelling a boom in informal economic activity that’s reshaping local landscapes. From trade and food stalls to mattress rentals, money transfers, horse-drawn carts and Jakarta motorbikes, these services are thriving and, by many accounts, highly profitable. In recent years, tourism infrastructure has also taken root, turning these transit zones into economic hotspots and accelerating the socio-spatial shifts behind the urbanisation - and rising land values - of Senegal’s border areas.

Conclusion

In the 21st century, the world has become essentially urban. Urbanisation, which reached its peak in the developed countries, is now occurring rapidly and anarchically in the countries of the Global South. Senegal, like other West African countries, is experiencing accelerated urbanisation, which is increasingly taking place in rural areas. This process is underpinned by several factors.

The crises in the rural world, which have led to a search for alternative livelihoods, have been accompanied by a major socio-spatial transformation or recomposition. The development of new sectors of activity fuelled by cross-border dynamics and town/country relations has had a dazzling impact on border villages. This is reflected in rapid spatial sprawl resulting from both intrinsic demographic dynamism and migratory influxes from inland villages and towns. Proximity to the secondary towns, ease of travel, the border effect and land accessibility are the driving forces behind the urbanisation process. As a result, while this urbanisation has raised the standard of living of rural dwellers, it can also be fertile ground for the development of phenomena such as food insecurity, lack of access to land and problems in planning and sanitation.

The views and analyses expressed here are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung.

Thousands of children in Gaza are grappling with the agony and disbelief of losing a parent.

The warmth and care of those who matter the most, stolen. No child should be left alone to fend for themself.
It is our responsibility and choice to stand by them now.

We are calling for donations to help us provide immediate relief and a lasting support system for 20,000 children.

Make a direct impact by sponsoring an orphan today.

Become an annual sponsor - $2,000

Become a monthly sponsor - $167

or choose your own amount, every contribution matters.

A full-scale humanitarian crisis needs an unmatched scale of support.

Here's how we are ramping up our efforts to ensure that donations will reach every orphan.

In partnership with Bank of Palestine Group, we have launched Noor’s Program to support 20,000 children orphaned by the war. Our target of 377 million dollars. to provide a comprehensive range of services that ensure these orphans can live with dignity, become active members of their communities, and build a better future for themselves.

We will be addressing several fronts from responding to immediate needs rising under the ongoing bombardment and aggression, to establishing a solid support system that the orphans can rely on until they reach the age of 18.

We have partnered with civil society organizations in Gaza that will help implement our various interventions, ensure direct access to the orphans and their families, as well as host activities in every locale. Meanwhile, our network of external experts will work alongside us to assess the program's needs, impact and progress.


This is our largest campaign for orphans to date. We count on every single contribution

Mohamed: A boy who lost everything,
but still found a reason to smile.

After losing his father and suffering severe injuries, Mohamed’s smile returned when he received new clothes. 'When I wore the new clothes, I felt like there’s someone out there who still cares,' he says.

Oday’s Vision Fades,
But Hope Remains

With the loss of his father and the sight in one eye, Oday faced darkness. Your support gave his family the essentials to restore hope for the future.

About Taawon

Taawon is an independent collective of Palestinian entrepreneurs, business practitioners, scholars and thinkers, bound together across generations by our dedication for Palestine to persevere and thrive.

Since 1983, we have worked to help defend and preserve the Palestinian cause, our culture and our people, by empowering Palestinians and investing in building Palestine's human capital together with local civil society organizations and a growing network of global support.

Over the last 15 years, Taawon has supported 4,261 orphans across Gaza, doing so in collaboration with a network of civil society organizations who specialize in these areas. The approach has always been focused on providing a holistic intervention encompassing education, finance and physical and mental health for each child based on their individual needs.

We are available for your inquiries.
Email us at [email protected] 

Gaza's orphaned children are our collective responsibility.

Thousands of orphaned children in Gaza are left heartbroken and lost, too young to understand the pain of losing their parents.

Their families, their warmth, their security—taken away in an instant. This Ramadan, let’s not let them face the darkness alone. It is our duty, our choice, to be the light they need.

Help us deliver urgent relief and develop a sustainable support system for 20,000 orphans in Gaza.

Taawon Foundation is an independent, non-profit Palestinian organization founded in Geneva in 1983 as a development institution aimed at enhancing the capabilities of the Palestinian people, preserving their heritage and identity, and supporting their vibrant culture. This is achieved through the systematic identification of the needs and priorities of the Palestinian people and employing appropriate mechanisms to maximize the use of available funding sources. The foundation implements its programs and interventions in partnership with a network of Palestinian civil society organizations that meet eligibility and due diligence requirements. It has offices in the West Bank, Gaza Strip, Jerusalem, and Lebanon, in addition to offices in Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and Jordan, which can receive funding and support through their bank accounts to finance programs within Palestine. So far, Taawon has successfully supported various development and relief projects and programs with a budget exceeding $950 million, aiming to invest in the Palestinian people, strengthen community resilience, and provide humanitarian support.

Be the change in an orphan’s life.
Sponsor today.

The warmth and care of those who matter the most, stolen. No child should be left alone to fend for themself.
It is our responsibility and choice to stand by them now.

We are calling for donations to help us provide immediate relief and a lasting support system for 20,000 children.

A full-scale humanitarian crisis needs an unmatched scale of support.

In partnership with Bank of Palestine Group, we have launched Noor’s Program to support 20,000 children orphaned by the war. Our target of 377 million dollars. to provide a comprehensive range of services that ensure these orphans can live with dignity, become active members of their communities, and build a better future for themselves.

Gaza is enduring relentless attacks.
Families are displaced, surviving without basic necessities.

Since the first day of the attack, Gaza has faced unthinkable suffering. Thousands of families are forced to survive in inhumane conditions, struggling without food, clean water, and basic healthcare.

It is our responsibility to stand by them now. Your donations would help us provide immediate relief for over 1.7 million displaced individuals. Help us ensure they receive the basic humanitarian needs.

Make a direct impact by contributing to Gaza’s urgent needs today.

The current reality at a glance..

1.7 Million Forcibly Displaced in a Small Area, Representing Only 10% of Gaza

Every day

63 families are displaced

1 out of 3

children in Gaza are malnourished

630,000

students deprived of attending school

Gaza is in crisis. An unprecedented scale of support is needed.

Here’s how we are responding to ensure aid reaches every family in need

Since the onset of the attack, more than half a million individuals have benefited from our interventions. Through the Gaza Emergency Relief Campaign, we are addressing urgent needs such as food, water, healthcare, and shelter for those displaced.

We have partnered with 20 local civil society organizations in Gaza to ensure direct access to displaced families and deliver aid in the toughest circumstances. Alongside our on-ground partners, our global network of supporters is working tirelessly to provide critical support for Gaza.

Areas of intervention

Food & Water

Food parcels &shopping vouchers, fresh produce parcels, and clean water

Healthcare

Medical supplies, and essential services, fuel for hospitals & ambulances

Shelter

Clothes, blankets, and emergency shelter materials

Mental Health Support

Essential Healthcare Services and social welfare

Majdi: A father supporting 8 family members while battling injury

After losing their home and struggling with injuries, your support provided them with essential clothing and hygiene kits, bringing comfort in difficult times.

Soha: A mother’s resilience builds a community kitchen.

Thanks to your support, Soha and her children managed to continue their work, providing 1,500 hot meals to displaced families through Taawon.

A family who lost everything yet refuses to give up.

Thanks to your support, Basem’s family received hygiene kits after losing their home in Gaza.

Shadi’s family finds warmth again

After losing their home and all their belongings, your support provided them with the clothes they need to stay warm.

Taawon

Taawon is an independent collective of Palestinian entrepreneurs, business practitioners, scholars and thinkers, bound together across generations by our dedication for Palestine to persevere and thrive. Since 1983, we have worked to help defend and preserve the Palestinian cause, our culture and our people, by empowering Palestinians and investing in building Palestine's human capital.

Together with local civil society organizations on the ground and a growing network of global support, we have managed to provide life-saving aid to Gaza's most vulnerable. Since the beginning of the attack on Gaza, our relief efforts have focused on providing food, shelter, medical aid, and mental health support to over 520,000 individuals in Gaza.

We are proud of our strong partnerships with more than 20 local organizations who ensure that aid reaches those who need it most, even in the most challenging conditions.

We are available for your inquiries.
Email us at [email protected]

Gaza’s families are counting on us.
Let’s stand by them today.

A crisis in Gaza's education needs an urgent response.

The education system in Gaza has been devastated by ongoing attacks, affecting the dreams and futures of over 88,000 students. Despite these challenges, the ISNAD program aims to provide 30,000 scholarships to support 15,000 students as well as university staff in Gaza, enabling them to resume their studies through distance learning.

The program focuses on major universities such as Al-Azhar University, the Islamic University, and Al-Aqsa University, which collectively serve 72% of Gaza's university students. With a target of raising $16,000,000, ISNAD will cover tuition fees for two semesters, ensuring educational continuity and giving these students the opportunity to build a better future for themselves and for Gaza, thereby enhancing the resilience of Palestinian universities to survive and thrive.

Make a direct impact. Support Gaza's education today. 

Sponsor one semester – $535

Sponsor one academic year – $1,070

Or choose your own amount – every contribution makes a difference.

Short Course on Palestine with Prof Rashid Khalidi

The Short Course on Palestine (September-October 2025), taught by Professor Rashid Khalidi and co-hosted by the People’s Forum and the Institute for Palestine Studies, offers an abbreviated examination of the history of Palestine since 1917…

ISNAD- Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1.    Who does ISNAD support?

ISNAD supports students enrolled in Gaza’s three public universities- Al Azhar, Al Aqsa, and the Islamic University- focusing on those in their final years of study. Priority is given to students in critical specialization that serve the emergency response and future reconstruction, such as health, engineering, education, and agriculture. It also supports students in digitally adaptable fields such as coding and digital marketing, helping them earn remotely and strengthen Gaza’s resilience.

2.    How is ISNAD different from other scholarship programs? 

ISNAD is tailored for crisis conditions. It not only supports students but also sustains Gaza’s public universities, operating through nationally endorsed mechanisms and targeting large-scale, urgent needs. It consolidates scattered emergency initiatives, scaling them into a structured, coordinated, and sustainable platform- aiming to become Palestine’s central scholarship mechanism. 

3.    Where does the donation go? 

All funds are transferred directly to universities through formal financial mechanisms approved by the Palestinian Monetary Authority, ensuring full transparency and accountability. 

4.    Is ISNAD endorsed by national authorities?

Yes. ISNAD operates under the umbrella of the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education and in partnership with Gaza’s major public universities. 

5.   Can individuals and institutions donate to ISNAD?

Yes. Both individuals and institutions can contribute. Donations can be made via Taawon’s website here, or by contacting our fundraising team for partnership opportunities at ([email protected] ).

6.    How is impact measured and reported? 

Through its steering committee and university representatives, Taawon monitors enrollment and graduation data, collects student surveys and testimonials, and receives university feedback and reports. 

7.    Why support students in Gaza’s universities instead of the emergency initiatives by universities themselves? 

ISNAD complements and coordinates partners' efforts under one structured, applicable national mechanism. ISNAD reduces duplication, ensures equal access, and aligns with Gaza’s reconstruction and educational recovery priorities. 

Scattered efforts can weaken impact; ISNAD scales them strategically. 
 

8.    What about internet access and digital barriers? 

ISNAD recognizes connectivity as a major barrier. ISNAD works closely with universities and local partners to provide flexible learning options and support, including printed materials, offline access tools, and targeted digital access solutions whenever possible, building on the lessons of COVID and the realities of the aggression. 

We are also seeking partnerships to establish internet access hubs and digital learning solutions across Gaza. 

9.    How does ISNAD operate amid Gaza’s famine and humanitarian crisis? 

ISNAD treats education as a lifeline, operating as an educational survival strategy- ensuring students remain connected to learning, purpose, and hope. Even amid famine, students attend remote classes and complete exams. ISNAD gives them a path forward when everything else is collapsing. 

10.    What is the long-term vision for ISNAD after the aggression? 

ISNAD seeks to prevent the collapse of Gaza’s higher education, and contributes to the steadfastness and resilience of national institutions by keeping students enrolled, supporting faculty, and preserving institutional continuity during aggression- laying the foundation for long-term recovery and development through (providing scholarship to majors that have direct impact to the current context and contributes to the reconstruction phase. 

11.    Why focus on the three public universities?

These universities make up 78% of Gaza’s student population, and are public institutions, public universities, relying on governmental finances to continue operating, which cannot happen in the current political landscape. 

About Taawon

Taawon is an independent collective of Palestinian entrepreneurs, business practitioners, scholars and thinkers, bound together across generations by our dedication for Palestine to persevere and thrive.
Since our establishment in 1983, Taawon has consistently worked to defend and preserve Palestinian culture and heritage, empowering communities and investing in human capital. Our interventions have included extensive support for the education sector, with $276,000,000 allocated to educational programs from 1983 to 2023. We work closely with local civil society organizations and a global support network to address the diverse needs of Palestinians.

We are available for your inquiries.
Email us at [email protected]
 

Don't let the aggression stop their educational journey

Education is a lifeline

Scholarships keep students on track, sustain Gaza’s universities and faculty, and protect the future of knowledge production in Palestine.

  • 20+ universities damaged
  • Direct payments to institutions

How ISNAD Works

Yes. Both individuals and institutions can contribute. Donations can be made via Taawon’s website here, or by contacting our fundraising team for partnership opportunities at ([email protected] ).

6.    How is impact measured and reported? 

Through its steering committee and university representatives, Taawon monitors enrollment and graduation data, collects student surveys and testimonials, and receives university feedback and reports. 

7.    Why support students in Gaza’s universities instead of the emergency initiatives by universities themselves? 

ISNAD complements and coordinates partners' efforts under one structured, applicable national mechanism. ISNAD reduces duplication, ensures equal access, and aligns with Gaza’s reconstruction and educational recovery priorities. 

Scattered efforts can weaken impact; ISNAD scales them strategically. 
 

8.    What about internet access and digital barriers? 

ISNAD recognizes connectivity as a major barrier. ISNAD works closely with universities and local partners to provide flexible learning options and support, including printed materials, offline access tools, and targeted digital access solutions whenever possible, building on the lessons of COVID and the realities of the aggression. 

We are also seeking partnerships to establish internet access hubs and digital learning solutions across Gaza. 

9.    How does ISNAD operate amid Gaza’s famine and humanitarian crisis? 

ISNAD treats education as a lifeline, operating as an educational survival strategy- ensuring students remain connected to learning, purpose, and hope. Even amid famine, students attend remote classes and complete exams. ISNAD gives them a path forward when everything else is collapsing. 

10.    What is the long-term vision for ISNAD after the aggression? 

ISNAD seeks to prevent the collapse of Gaza’s higher education, and contributes to the steadfastness and resilience of national institutions by keeping students enrolled, supporting faculty, and preserving institutional continuity during aggression- laying the foundation for long-term recovery and development through (providing scholarship to majors that have direct impact to the current context and contributes to the reconstruction phase. 

11.    Why focus on the three public universities?

These universities make up 78% of Gaza’s student population, and are public institutions, public universities, relying on governmental finances to continue operating, which cannot happen in the current political landscape. 

About Taawon

Taawon is an independent collective of Palestinian entrepreneurs, business practitioners, scholars and thinkers, bound together across generations by our dedication for Palestine to persevere and thrive.
Since our establishment in 1983, Taawon has consistently worked to defend and preserve Palestinian culture and heritage, empowering communities and investing in human capital. Our interventions have included extensive support for the education sector, with $276,000,000 allocated to educational programs from 1983 to 2023. We work closely with local civil society organizations and a global support network to address the diverse needs of Palestinians.

We are available for your inquiries.

Al-Bireh, Palestine — 1 September 2026 — Taawon (Welfare Association), Inash Al-Usra Association, and the Palestinian Museum have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to collaborate on a new art project entitled “When the Canvas Weaves into the Thobe.” The partnership brings together three institutions that have each sustained ongoing efforts to preserve Palestinian cultural life, now join forces on a shared project where embroidery meets painting.

The collection features six embroidered thobes inspired by the paintings of renowned artist Suleiman Mansour, creating a dynamic dialogue between two distinct Palestinian artistic traditions: fine art and traditional embroidery. Selected details from Mansour’s decades-long portfolio depicting the Palestinian landscape and its people are translated into thread and fabric — a medium long used by Palestinian women across generations to record place, belonging, and identity.

Rather than simply reproducing the paintings, the craft reinterprets Mansour's work. Through this exchange, embroidery becomes a medium through which his art finds new expression, creating a bridge between past and present and affirming the continuity of Palestinian culture within contemporary practice.

Under the agreement, the three institutions will work together to develop, exhibit, and promote the collection through partnerships with international museums and cultural institutions, host exhibitions, and organize tours both within Palestine and abroad.

For Taawon, this partnership extends a commitment that runs through all of its work: that Palestinian identity, heritage, and cultural memory are not simply to be archived, but are living practices carried forward by each generation. The collaboration sits within Taawon’s wider mission — investing in people, sustaining communities, and responding to humanitarian need — where cultural continuity is a vital part of community resilience.

Every child deserves the opportunity to grow up surrounded by care, protected with dignity, and given the chance to look toward the future with hope. Yet since October 2023, the war in Gaza has left more than 58,000 children without one or both parents, creating an unprecedented need for sustained care and protection.

The Justice Company Humanitarian Foundation https://www.justicecompanyfoundation.com/, supported by The Justice Company www.justicecompany.com, supports carefully selected humanitarian initiatives that expand opportunity, strengthen resilience, and improve outcomes for vulnerable individuals and communities. Through this commitment, the Foundation has partnered with Taawon to support 250 orphaned children in Gaza through the NOOR Orphan Care Program.

Developed by Taawon in response to the war in Gaza, the NOOR Orphan Care Program is built on the belief that no child should have to face such profound loss alone. More than a sponsorship programme, NOOR is a comprehensive, long-term initiative that combines immediate humanitarian support with long-term human development. Through healthcare, education, humanitarian assistance, mental health and psychosocial support, and social care, the programme walks alongside children throughout their journey, helping them heal, regain stability, remain protected, and build a future filled with dignity and hope.

The Foundation's support reflects a shared belief that children who have experienced profound loss deserve more than short-term assistance. They deserve the opportunity to continue learning, recover in a safe and supportive environment, and grow into healthy, resilient young people despite the extraordinary challenges they have faced.

For the 250 children supported through this partnership, NOOR represents far more than humanitarian assistance. It offers continuity of care, stability, and the reassurance that they are not alone, that someone is walking beside them, investing in their wellbeing, and helping them shape a brighter future.

Together, the Foundation and Taawon are investing in more than meeting today's needs. They are helping restore hope, strengthen resilience, and ensure that orphaned children have the opportunity to heal, thrive, and build the future they deserve.

NOOR is Taawon's flagship national initiative for the care of Gaza's orphaned children, providing an integrated model of support that accompanies children from emergency response through long-term recovery and development.

Our development team offers one-to-one consultations for filmmakers based in Qatar, providing tailored creative support across all stages of a project’s evolution.

Whether you are shaping an initial idea, refining a script, or preparing a project for production, our sessions are designed to help you strengthen your story, deepen your vision, and identify your next creative steps.

We work exclusively with filmmakers who have been living in Qatar for at least one year.

During the consultation, our team engages directly with your material—be it a concept note, a script draft, or a developed pitch. Based on your needs, we provide feedback on narrative structure, character development, visual storytelling, and thematic clarity.

Our goal is to empower storytellers with the insight and support needed to move forward with purpose and confidence.

Interested in a consultation?

Please email development@dohafilm.com with:

  • A brief overview of your project
  • Its current stage of development
  • Areas where you would like support
  • A copy of your QID

We look forward to hearing from you soon!

Mustafa, 14-years old student at Dar Al-Aytam School in Al-Thawri neighborhood in Jerusalem. Several months ago, he was one of the students who were known for their lack of discipline and commitment to the educational process. This situation turned when he joined the "For my identity, I sing" project which aims to strengthen the Palestinian cultural identity for students in Jerusalem schools.Mustafa became very engaged with the project and became more committed to the learning process, which was clearly reflected in his academic achievements. More importantly, during the program, he demonstrated a keen interest in music. The project motivated Mustafa's positive behavior as he was one of the most violent students towards people and objects. He used to bother his colleagues, the education staff and even the school's guests.

Today, Mustafa is confident in what he does, he found that he could express himself decently and treat others with respect. He no longer needs to prove anything to anyone; he became interested in expressing himself through rap music, which made the anger he used to experience almost disappear.

The Project Coordinator, Ms. Rawan Ghneim, said that "For My Identity, I sing" project aims to help the students form their personal and national identity and provides them with skills and tools which help them express their views on issues of interest to them, through different creative methods. 

Through the project, 16 meetings for each group were implemented in three Jerusalem schools, which were attended by 58 students. In the cultural groups they formed, the students went through intensive training and each group produced a song from their own words. The project also worked on enabling and developing teacher and consultant abilities and skills for 24 public schools in Jerusalem in utilizing music and arts in different school activities.

In addition, 24 teachers were trained in designing plans for free activities, art performances, and experimental applications. In the schools were teachers were trained, the project followed the implementation of activities and distributed 25 kits with materials used for art activities to these schools. Ms. Ghneim adds "The project affected students positively, as they have now a space to express themselves, increase their confidence, and discover the talents and skills they have been inside them, in addition to music education." 

Ahmed Safadi, the director of Al-Aytam School, confirmed that he interacted with the project from its beginning, and he was very enthusiastic to join even though it was the first time the school dealt with a team specialized in teaching musical arts. He adds: "The students were able to form a collective song and sing it in front of the Parents' Council and during the school radio. This increased their confidence and reflected in their participation in different activities and they won the third place in the theater competition." He pointed out that regarding the current political situation of the Palestinian schools in Jerusalem; the students enrolled in the project proved the national identity through the national song. 

Mr. Safadi continues: "Students want to continue this project, especially that private schools are distinguished from public schools with their extracurricular activities. I hope the project will be able to break the routine of the curriculum through new educational tools. 

We thank the Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development; I appreciate the professionalism of "Taawon" in supervising projects. I hope that the experiment will be circulated to all schools so that the talents of young people can be developed.”

"For my identity, I sing" is implemented by "Al-Mada" organization in cooperation with the Ministry of Education, funded by the Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development and the support of Taawon.

Al-Khalidiya Library, an ancient building that dates to the thirteenth century AD, is at the heart of the city of Jerusalem, one hundred meters away from Al-Aqsa Mosque in the “Bab Alsilsila” or Chain Gate area and overlooks the western wall and the Dung Gate or “Bab Al Magharbeh.” Throughout the years, its stones became witnesses to several successive rules starting from the Umayyad period, passing through the Ottoman period, and ending with the Israeli occupation. It is, which contains an enormous collection of ancient books as well as significant and exceptional manuscripts that were owned by Al-Khalidi Family.

In the year of 1900, Haj Ragheb Al-Khalidi established the Khalidiya Library after he realized that the books are being distributed across the houses of Al-Khalidi family members and are being inherited. Thus, he established the library in order to bring all the collection together under one roof and in fear of its loss.

The library has 1209 manuscripts entailing about two thousand titles in various sciences, some of which are presented in colored ink and decorated with geometric motifs and shapes. Among these manuscripts are 200 rare Islamic manuscripts, according to Dr.  Assem Khalidi, a member of Al-Khalidi Endowment committee.

One of these rare manuscripts is “Abundance of commendation, parterre of pride and influence of the characteristics of Al-Nasser the king”. The manuscript is over 800 years old, in particular, a few years post the death of Salah Al-Deen Al-Ayyoubi in 1193.

This cultural oasis, preserving between its walls and coffers Arab and Islamic history and civilization, suffered from the lack of financial resources, not to mention the need of the building and books for urgent restoration and renovation. To achieve that goal, the library continues to cooperate with Taawon, which in turn responded to the needs of the library, and believed in the significance of this place, which contains a large part of Arab heritage in the Holy City.

Dr. Khader Salameh, the Technical Director of the Khalidiya library says that, the restoration project is funded by the Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development and supervised and implemented by Taawon; it is divided into two components, a cultural component which is executed through the provision of sources of books and the development of library work, and the other is architectural, which aims to restore the historic library building. He extended his thanks to the Arab Fund for its generous support in preserving the library and developing its work. He also thanked Taawon which worked on restoring the building with high professionalism and contributed to the development of the library.

This support is very essential as it preserves human heritage that demonstrates the culture of the Palestinian society that is prevalent at the time; it also works to develop the assets for future generations to benefit from, as well as to help spread the library's manuscripts and rare resources.

On the architectural side, Taawon has developed an executive plan for the restoration of the Khalidiya library and its extension. According to Engineer Bashar Al-Husseini, Director of restoration projects at Taawon, the project was divided into three phases; the first phase included the main library building and is expected to be completed in September 2018. The second phase, which was completed and included the restoration of the main facade of the library, also contained elements of the architectural characteristic of five historical eras. As for the third phase, its implementation will begin at the end of 2018 to strengthen and rehabilitate the library supplement, which suffers from structural problems evident by several fractures and cracks. Al-Husseini explains that the renovation of Al-Khalidiya library is in accordance with international standards yet using traditional materials suitable for historical buildings and according to the requirements of the library.

As for the cultural component, provided by Taawon, it includes the restoration of manuscripts, purchasing new books, producing displays and mobile shelves for books and manuscripts, as well as establishing an indexing system, and organizing the opening of the library in later periods to benefit any researcher interested in the history of Palestine in general and the history of Jerusalem in particular.

Dr. Salamah expressed his hope that the Arab Fund and Taawon would continue to provide support to the Khalidiya library as it is one of the city's precious treasures. He concluded: “The identity of Jerusalem is the identity of all Arabs and its preservation is the duty of everyone who respects and appreciates civilization, science, and culture.”

items.content_html:
The story of Fadi Al Dihleez

Al Dihleez family lives in Gaza, their home is in very poor condition as a result of the military bombardment in the summer of 2014. Their small home has cracked walls and ceilings, which they couldn’t afford to fix yet. The house is subject to continuous flooding every time it rains and flooding from the street  and the nearby sanitation station.  Mr. Dihleez takes care of his 70- year old mother in addition to his wife and children. He is unemployed and has been looking for a job for the past few years with no luck. He relies on assistance from the Ministry of Social Affairs’ (MoSA. He receives occasional supplementary assistance from local NGOs. The family are surviving on less than US$100 per month that barely covers their key daily needs.

Fadi’s family was one of the recipients of the “Emergency Winterisation Support for Families in Gaza” project, which is funded by IDRF and Welfare Association. They received two blankets and chose three sets of winter clothes for their children at a pre-qualified store. Fadi said “I was unable to provide my kids with winter clothes. Your help came at the right time to prevent my children from getting sick with the flu and cold. The situation of my family continues to deteriorate, and your help really makes a difference. Thank you”. This Winterization project has benefited 179 families in Gaza up to date.

Story of Rawheya Abu Jazar

Mrs. Rawheya Abu Jazar, is a 53-year old mother, taking care of her seven children alone. Rawheya and her family live in a small home in very difficult conditions in Al Shoka, east of Rafah, in Gaza. She has nowhere else to go.

Rawheya has no source of income at all. She relies on assistance from relatives and neighbours. The two older children (a boy and a girl in secondary school) left school due to financial inability to cover the costs of uniform, books and transport. items.title: Stories from the Field – Gaza Winterization Project
items.summary:
The story of Fadi Al Dihleez

Al Dihleez family lives in Gaza, their home is in very poor condition as a result of the military bombardment in the summer of 2014. Their small home has cracked walls and ceilings, which they couldn’t afford to fix yet. The house is subject to continuous flooding every time it rains and flooding from the street  and the nearby sanitation station.  Mr. Dihleez takes care of his 70- year old mother in addition to his wife and children. He is unemployed and has been looking for a job for the past few years with no luck. He relies on assistance from the Ministry of Social Affairs’ (MoSA. He receives occasional supplementary assistance from local NGOs. The family are surviving on less than US$100 per month that barely covers their key daily needs.

Fadi’s family was one of the recipients of the “Emergency Winterisation Support for Families in Gaza” project, which is funded by IDRF and Welfare Association. They received two blankets and chose three sets of winter clothes for their children at a pre-qualified store. Fadi said “I was unable to provide my kids with winter clothes. Your help came at the right time to prevent my children from getting sick with the flu and cold. The situation of my family continues to deteriorate, and your help really makes a difference. Thank you”. This Winterization project has benefited 179 families in Gaza up to date.

items.content_html:
Educational innovation

Rami Felfel, founder of the (Innovation of Education) was a high school teacher in the Gaza strip, and has felt difficulties that students suffer when they study for the final tawjihi year where they try to collect materials and tests from their friends and are unable to know when they have answered correctly or not.

“We wanted to develop an electronic exam platform that includes a variety of question types, and provides immediate feedback to students so that they can learn faster and more effectively, and link with their teachers quicker” said Felfel.

To realise this, Fefel and his co-founder has joined “Riyada” project that has facilitated the establishment and empowerment of 13+ startups in ICT and relevant sectors, supported from Human Appeal UK, and implemented via Taawon in partnership with the Islamic University of Gaza’s BTI incubator.

He added that their startup, (Innovation of Education), has developed an online platform called "Smart Test", which provides educational and mentoring services for all educational fields, provides intelligence measurement services and special programs for gifted students, and aims to facilitate the difficulty students face in their final high school years and facilitate and improve their learning experience.

 Last month, the startup has held the first computerized Biology exam for students of the 11th grade at AlKarmel Public High School, where students were very engaged and happy with this new experience.

Nader Abdulnabi, Riyada Project coordinator, said that (Innovation of Education) has held the electronic test at Alkramel High School for about 40 students who were tested in an electronic suitable environment for 45 minutes, where they could immediately see how they performed while their marks were passed to their teachers.

Fahad Al-Din Muhanna, a teacher of the biology course at Alkarmel High School, stressed that the project facilitates the design of the tests and saves a lot of time and effort in the marking and revision process. He pointed out the flexibility of the system in designing the test in accordance with the students' levels through a variety of questions as it enables students to read their results graphically, which helps in determining, analyzing and comparing student levels and weak points.

Innovation in translation and languages

Another startup benefiting from Riyada project is “Al Farabi”, an emerging startup from Gaza working in multilingual translation services that provides translation services to 18 languages ​​worldwide.

It seems almost impossible for two young men who have not yet graduated, but they have already taken significant steps towards their childhood dream, their translation startup “Al-Farabi”

In 2016, Anas Abu Samhan and Hossam Tanira (24) have graduated from the university with an idea in mind. Anas explained that the idea of ​​the translation project began to crystallize when he saw a man with signs of sadness on his face while he was look at a non-Arabic medical report of his sick daughter and unable to understand what it said, which led to the passion and love of translation stronger with Anas.

Anas, a graduate of the Faculty of Arts, Department of English at the Islamic University, says: "During the past five years, I tried to establish relationships with a number of translators on Facebook, so I later managed to create a wide network of translators worldwide."

"At first, I was afraid of creating an integrated team in the Gaza Strip for Al-Farabi because there was no place equipped with computers and the Internet. Once he and his cofounder has joined Riyada project, they were able to receive hosting and incubation services, as well as the financial and mentorship support by the project.

"The financial return of Al-Farabi's translation project has doubled after providing the team has received an incubation space and support services from “Riyada”.

Hossam adds: "Translation requires skills to be enhanced, improved, and become more readable. This will help benefit more customers ". He mentions that In a short period of time, the team was able to translate eight books, a number of articles, poetry, scientific papers, and researches. One of these books was sold to a Kuwaiti publishing house for mass printing.

items.content_html:
Azizah is a mother of five daughters and one boy living in difficult conditions inside a Caravan. Aziza has chronic diseases, namely diabetes and hypertension. Azizah is a widow as she lost her husband a long time ago. She also lost her son in the assault on Gaza 12 years ago. She took the responsibility for the whole family ever-since. The burden on Azizah has increased following the year 2014 when the family’s home was demolished and they live temporarily ever-since in a caravan in Bait Hanoun awaiting reconstruction.

Azizah supports her family’s from assistance provided by the Ministry of Social Affairs - as she lost a son in the 2014 assault on Gaza. However, this assistance is not sufficient any way. Azizah was selected by Taawon project team in coordination with local organizations to benefit from the weekly fresh food parcels, for three weeks.

With support of Human Appeal, Taawon provided Azizah with fresh food parcels to contribute towards improving the family’s food security. The parcels brought about some happiness to the family especially the kids.

While she is very thankful for this support Aziza still needs all types of assistance to enable her and her family to survive.

It is worth noting that the fresh food parcels were procured from needy small farmers in Gaza in order to support their businesses and contribute to improving their economic conditions.

items.content_html:
Alaa Al Dahdouh is a Palestinian farmer who owns a small greenhouse in Gaza. General conditions in Gaza are affecting Alaa and his family directly since the selling prices of their products have dwindled due to the low purchasing power of customers. On the other hand, the Gaza closure has driven up the cost of agricultural inputs. The marketing of farmer products and cash collections from wholesalers are very difficult given the dire economic conditions.

Alaa supports an extended family consisting of 10 members including five boys and three girls, one of whom is studying at the university. One of his daughters has health problems and had underwent open-heart and requires good care, medications with significant cost, but Alaa takes good care of her. Alaa also takes care of his elderly mother. Alaa raised his brothers after his father passed away years ago. Alaa was a child then, and he took the responsibility of the whole family.

Taawon team, in coordination with the Agricultural Committees, nominated Alaa as a supplier for its family sponsorship project supported by Human Appeal. The project team visited Alaa and determined the agricultural products he can supply. Alaa had supplied his vegetables, in previous years, to similar projects and his products were excellent.

Through this project, a small quantity of Alaa’s agricultural crops are purchased at a reasonable price allowing him to maintain his livelihood and support his family. The project bought 0.7 tons of tomatoes from Alaa to be distributed as part of fresh food parcels to needy families. In his words:

“I have been selected to provide tomatoes for this project and this really helped me to market my tomatoes and give the families the production without the burden of going to the local market.

Thank you for your support.”

items.content_html:
To most of the participants in the Zyara program, this was their first trip to Palestine. Their prior knowledge was limited to what they had read or heard about in the media, where Palestine is usually portrayed only as a war zone. Zyara participants were given the opportunity to witness the different restrictions that limit the movement of Palestinians and affect every aspect of their life through the combinations of different checkpoints, the separation wall, refugee camps, and illegal settlements. The trip provided the participants with the opportunity to live Palestine and to experience its beautiful cultural heritage, including visiting key historical and religious sites and tasting local traditional food.

Youssef Salhi, a professor of Arabic at Georgia Southern University, and of Moroccan origin, has always been a huge fan of Mahmoud Darwish’s work and has included many of the poet’s works in his lectures. During his visit to Palestine, Youssef had the opportunity to visit the Mahmoud Darwish Museum and learn more about the poet’s life and work, inspiring him to dedicate a whole class to Darwish’s writings in the upcoming semester. 

Kris Koenig, a filmmaker from California, has been working on a project entitled “Sticks and Stones: Adolescent PTSD and the Middle East Conflict”. Before Kris’s trip to Palestine, the idea of the film was to give a voice to the children who have lost their childhoods to trauma and violence, and to show the medical and psychological impacts of PTSD (Post-traumatic Stress Disorder) on the human body. Zyara introduced Kris to Accountability for Violence Against Children (AVAC), an organization which sheds light on the violations that cause children and their families in Palestine much suffering. The program provides psychotherapy and legal support free of charge, as well as legal follow-ups, to reinforce the people’s rights and limit future violations. Kris was very impressed by AVAC’s work and decided to make them the focus of his film.

Zyara is a cultural exchange program that aims to introduce US citizens, including academics, journalists, physicians, lawyers, and people of faith, to the political and socioeconomic situation in Palestine, and provide them with opportunities to meet and interact with Palestinians from all walks of life in order to better understand the Palestinian perspective and the political realities of their daily life. Zyara takes into consideration the participants’ areas of interests when planning the trips. The program is implemented by Taawon, in partnership with the American Federation of Ramallah-Palestinewith funding from the Bank of Palestine and the United Palestinian Appeal.

Ahmad, 12 years, is an orphan from Gaza and bene ciary of the Wajd Orphan Support Program. The co-curricular activities held by Wajd, gave Ahmad the chance to express himself through arts and uncovered his amazing talent for drawing portraits. Ahmad is receiving a holistic array of services including education support and health care from Wajd which will continue to support him until he is 22 years old. ‘Wajd” is funded by Qatar Fund for Development, Bank of Palestine and the Haj Hashim Al-Shawa Charitable Fund.

Ahmad said, “I wish everyone would see my talent and how it improved. I am so happy and I will keep learning until I become an important artist.”

items.content_html:
The story of Hanan, 14 years old, began a few years ago when her mother noticed in her daughter a slight bend in her back when she stood up. As Hanan grew, this curve soon increased significantly, accompanied by difficulties in walking and breathing. Hanan was diagnosed with severe sprain in the spine, which exceeded 60 degrees. Surgical intervention was the only solution for this condition, a delicate and costly intervention. “I had reached a point where I could no longer do anything to save my daughter's life,” says Hanan's mother. "But I had hope."

The cost of the surgery was beyond our ability to pay for it, adds Hanan's mother, saying, "At this point, parents feel helpless, and that is a very difficult feeling." In less than a year, the convolutedness in Hanan’s spine had increased to more than 70 degrees. There was a real danger to her lungs. She was forced to stop going to school, and we realized then that it was urgent that something was done. "Hanan's medical file was one of the emergency files being followed by UNRWA, and all our hopes rested on their aid."

"My daughter was given a new chance after more than six hours in the surgery room, and Hanan was able to walk again... My joy is indescribable. It is hard to express my deepest gratitude and thanks to all those who have helped my daughter to be reborn.”

The campaign launched by Taawon-Lebanon with UNRWA during Ramadan succeeded in raising the needed amount to complete a delicate spinal operation to save Hanan. The surgery was successful, and Hanan was able to walk again after she left the hospital.

The cost of the operation was US$31,600 and was covered by donations of more than US$10,000 from Taawon-Lebanon, US$5,000 from the Palestine Relief Society, US$12,000 from Al-Kuwait Red Crescent, US$2,500 from the Palestine Liberation Organization, US$1,250 from the Health Care Association, and US$800 from the Zakat Fund.

Thanks to everyone who helped save Hanan's life, and for your warm hearts and your kind and generous gifts!
